Lexicon vīvum · 270 grouped entries · updated 29 October 2026

Lexicon Latīnitātis Cotīdiānae

Everyday Latin for conversation, family routines and play with Theo. Long vowels carry macrons; uncertain loanword quantities and our own modern formations are clearly identified.

Macrons, usage and evidence

Macrons mark long vowels; short vowels are left plain. A heavy syllable is not automatically a long vowel. Consonantal i is written j (jam, ejus, conjungō), and the vowel before intervocalic j is left unmarked (major); search treats i and j alike. Inflected examples, genitives, principal parts and Latin headings are included in the review.

For ancient vocabulary, the main references are Lewis & Short and Lewis’s Elementary Latin Dictionary through Perseus and Logeion, with Dickinson’s core list for cross-checking. Hidden quantities are also compared against Bennett’s discussion with Michelson’s corrections and notes on Allen. Dictionary omissions are not automatically proof of shortness; disputed lengths are identified where relevant.

Bulgarian translations accompany the construction, workshop and house-layout vocabulary reviewed on 24 October 2026; search accepts all three languages.

For modern words, the classical lengths of inherited roots and regular Latin endings are retained where justified. Loanword stem quantities that the checked sources do not establish are explicitly labelled. “Reading convention” marks an adopted reconstruction, rather than an attested ancient pronunciation.

Ancient Latin means the word and its relevant basic sense are ancient. Lexicographic evidence means a modern dictionary records the expression; it does not imply universal acceptance. Modern extension applies an older word to a modern object. Working formation identifies our own phrase or name adaptation.

Example sentences are composed for conversation with Theo. They are not quotations unless an author and passage are identified. Noun genitives and genders, important sense distinctions, and known alternative forms are supplied where useful.

Review notes · 29 October 2026

All 53 original grouped entries were reviewed; 39 household and family entries were added. Quantities, examples, definitions and attestation labels were checked separately. The review also removes unsupported precise dates, unsourced principal parts and blanket “attested” tags.

5 October 2026 addition: three family-play entries cover trampoline jumping, Sīmius et arbor and Nauta et undae. The game titles and spoken prompts are our own; modern senses are labelled. The plural genua has short u.

7 October 2026 addition: ausum is the preferred ancient word for “adventure” in the sense of a daring undertaking or venture; adventūra is retained as a medieval/modern alternative, with its semantic development explicitly noted.

11 October 2026 addition: seven workshop-and-repair entries distinguish ancient tool vocabulary from later technical Latin and our own descriptive formations. The review replaces the earlier unsupported cochleārius for “screwdriver” with lexicographically attested vertitōrium, prefers forceps for pliers, records variable vowel quantity in cochlea and terebra, and distinguishes English “dowel” (scalmus) from Bulgarian дюбел. For the latter, ancora mūrālis plastica is explicitly marked as our provisional descriptive formation, not as an attested traditional term.

18 October 2026 addition: 27 grouped entries cover the family smoothie guide: ingredients, equipment, materials, measurements, preparation verbs and phrases for cooking with Theodōrus. Traupman’s uploaded Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, Morgan–Owens and ancient dictionaries were compared. Recorded modern terms, older words with modern senses, uncertain quantities and our composed descriptions are labelled separately. Start with smoothie ingredients · Source audit.

24 October 2026 addition: 17 grouped entries cover construction, house layout, furnishings, trowels, a crowbar, extension leads, cable reels and sheet-metal shears. Existing workshop entries were extended with Bulgarian terminology and the recorded tape-measure phrase. Descriptive formations and uncertain ancient senses remain explicit. Construction vocabulary source audit.

24 October 2026 addition: 17 grouped entries cover hooks, swinging, pipes, gravel, movement, flips, trenches, dirt, heaps, squeezing/crushing, crashes, missions/quests, caps, scaffolding and its parts/actions. Eight existing entries were extended or cross-linked for rods/bars, blankets, lids, planks, wiping and food-preparation verbs. This batch adds English–Latin vocabulary only. Physical senses, modern applications and our composed descriptions remain distinct. Site and play vocabulary source audit.

25 October 2026: a dedicated Lūdī et lūdibria category adds 14 grouped playground/toy entries and brings the existing swing entry into the same filter. Playground source audit.

26 October 2026: classical sources and corrections for the site and construction vocabulary. Two entries are added: the adze, ascia, and ground level, basement, terrace, wing and extension. Scaffolding now leads with māchina and Vitruvius’s arrēctāria / trānsversāria; norma is written without a macron; coctilis has a short i. tabula spūmea is our working formation for EPS board. Site vocabulary corrections.

29 October 2026: the sitting room is exedra (Vitruvius, Cicero; Traupman p. 125), not sessōrium, whose ancient senses are “seat” and, in one passage of Petronius, “dwelling”; concrete is opus caementīcium, after Vitruvius’s caementīcius, not Traupman’s concrētum; jentāculum and jentō have a short e, as Lewis & Short leaves them.

29 October 2026 addition: the daily-life vocabulary of the seven fābulae Theodōrus et pater (I Iter in Lūsitāniam to VII Diēs ūnus Osoitsae), first proposed on 23 October and rebased on the revised texts: 75 grouped entries (entry-196 to entry-270) cover travel, town and shops, place names, weather and landscape, trees, animals, market food, kitchen work, the house and its rebuilding, and phrases for the day with Theodōrus. A new category, Urbs, vīcus et loca, holds town, shop and place-name vocabulary. Where a proposed card duplicated an existing one (body parts, vegetables, playground, slide, swing, sandpit, ball games, balance bike, rooms, builders, building timber, family, and the adze card of 26 October), its new words and examples were added to that card instead. Every example marked “Fābula” was re-quoted from the texts as revised on 29 October, in their j orthography. The fork is furcilla (not fuscinula), and mantēle leads with its classical sense, the hand towel. Corrections made on 23 October: jentāculum (short e), būtȳrum, pōtiō, lac, lacūna, īnstrūmentum, vēsīca īnflāta and ēlectricus; alternatives were added to the coffee, tram, trampoline, stick, back, balloon, wake-up, hug, pepper, pumpkin, cutting-board, peel and berry entries. Search fabulae to see the addition.

Selected quantity corrections
  • ramus / ramulus / ramos → rāmus / rāmulus / rāmōs
  • gravedō / gravedinis → gravēdō / gravēdinis
  • involucrum / manubrium → involūcrum / manūbrium
  • scabī / vesīca / semita → scābī / vēsīca / sēmita
  • vaccinium / morum → vaccīnium / mōrum
  • frīgeō / algēō / fervēō / languēō → frīgeō / algeō / ferveō / langueō
  • elaborātiō / recognitiō → ēlabōrātiō / recōgnitiō
  • program(m)ātum as a noun genitive plural → programmatum; verbal programmātum is a different form
Usage corrections

Ancient fermentō, fermentēscō and vapōrō are no longer called exclusively later inventions. Berry names distinguish modern botanical use from uncertain ancient identification. Totoro, the magnetic-toy phrase and specific Git phrases are labelled as our own adaptations.

The kettle expression and unsupported yogurt or coffee stem quantities are described with their actual level of evidence. Source links appear inside each entry.

Body, health & movement

Corpus et mōtus

12 entries

Scratch

scabō, scabere, scābī

Ancient Latin
  • scabō, scabere, scābī — scratch or scrape; no attested supine is supplied in Lewis & Short.
  • scalpō, scalpere, scalpsī, scalptum — scratch, scrape, carve, engrave.
  • scabiēs f. — an itching or scabby skin condition; mange. It is broader than the modern diagnosis “scabies.” The classical dictionaries give accusative scabiem and ablative scabiē, without supplying a genitive.
  • scaber, scabra, scabrum — rough, scabby.
  • Nōlī scabere. — Don’t scratch.
  • scrībō, scrībere, scrīpsī, scrīptum — write; historically associated with scratching or incising. English script belongs to this family.
Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: scabo · Lewis & Short: scalpo · Lewis & Short: scabies · Lewis & Short: scribo

Itch

prūriō, prūrīre

Ancient Latin
  • prūriō, prūrīre — itch; also figuratively long for something. The ancient dictionary does not supply a perfect or supine; regular-looking perfects are not presented as verified principal parts.
  • prūrītus, prūrītūs m. — itching; prūrīgō, prūrīginis f. — itching, irritation.
  • prūriēns, prūrientis — itching.
  • Mihi bracchium prūrit. — My arm itches.
  • Ubi tibi prūrit? — Where does it itch?
  • English medical pruritus derives from the Latin noun; the verb’s further etymology is uncertain.
Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: prurio · Lewis & Short: pruritus · Lewis & Short: prurigo

Pop / burst

crepō, crepāre, crepuī, crepitum

Ancient wordsModern extension
  • crepō, crepāre, crepuī, crepitum — crack, pop, make a sharp noise.
  • rumpō, rumpere, rūpī, ruptum — break, burst, rupture; transitive, or passive when something bursts.
  • crepitus, crepitūs m. — cracking or popping sound; crepitō, crepitāre, crepitāvī, crepitātum — crackle repeatedly.
  • vēsīca, vēsīcae f. — bladder; extended here to an inflated balloon. vēsīca īnflāta makes the image explicit.
  • follis īnflātus — balloon, from follis, a bag or inflated ball (L&S).
  • Vēsīca crepat. — The balloon pops.
  • Vēsīcam rumpe. — Burst the balloon.
  • English rupture, interrupt, corrupt belong to the rumpō family. crepō is usually treated as imitative.

Common cold / feeling cold

gravēdō, gravēdinis f.

Ancient Latin
  • gravēdō, gravēdinis f. — heaviness, especially a cold in the head or catarrh; useful for “a cold,” without claiming an exact ancient diagnosis of a modern viral infection.
  • corȳza, corȳzae f. — catarrh; a Greek medical loan, attested in Late Latin.
  • dēstīllātiō, dēstīllātiōnis f. — dripping or discharge; catarrh in medical contexts.
  • frīgus, frīgoris n. — coldness, not normally the illness; frīgeō, frīgēre — be cold; algeō, algēre, alsī — feel cold.
  • Gravēdinem habeō. — I have a cold.
  • Gravēdine labōrō. — I’m suffering from a cold.
  • Nāsus fluit. — The nose is running.
  • Nāsus obstructus est. — The nose is blocked.
  • gravēdō is formed from gravis, “heavy”; corȳza represents Greek κόρυζα.
Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: gravedo · Lewis & Short: coryza · Lewis & Short: destillatio · Lewis & Short: frigus · Lewis & Short: algeo · Bennett: hidden quantities, with later corrections

Body parts for washing / dressing / fingers / eyes / face

manus, manūs f.

Ancient Latin
  • caput, capitis n. — head; auris, auris f. — ear; ōs, ōris n. — mouth; collum, collī n. — neck.
  • bracchium, bracchiī n. — arm; cubitum, cubitī n. — elbow; manus, manūs f. — hand.
  • pēs, pedis m. — foot; crūs, crūris n. — lower leg; genū, genūs n. — knee.
  • venter, ventris m. — belly; dorsum, dorsī n.; tergum, tergī n. — back; umerus, umerī m. — shoulder.
  • Manum mihi dā. — Give me your hand.
  • Pedes lavēmus. — Let’s wash our feet.
  • Ubi genū tuum est? — Where is your knee?
  • digitus, digitī m. — finger; oculus, oculī m. — eye; frōns, frontis f. — forehead; pectus, pectoris n. — chest.
  • vultus, vultūs m. — face, expression; vultum dūcere — pull a face; ōs contrahere — pucker one’s mouth. sūdō, sūdāre, sūdāvī, sūdātum — sweat.
  • Quīnque digitōs ostendere cōnātus, trēs ostendit. — Trying to show five fingers, he showed three. (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).

Move (noun) / movement / game move

mōtus, mōtūs m.; tractus, tractūs m.

Ancient nounRecorded game sense
  • mōtus, mōtūs m. — movement; our general choice for a physical or dance move when context makes the particular action clear.
  • mōtus and tractus, tractūs m. — recorded by Morgan–Owens for a move of a playing piece or checker. A game move need not be described as an ordinary bodily movement.
  • Hunc mōtum imitāre. — Copy this move. Mōtūs tuōs spectō. — I’m watching your movements. These examples are composed, not quotations.

Flip over / flip (noun) / somersault

invertō, invertere; saltus cernuus

Ancient verbsRecorded gymnastic sense
  • invertō, invertere, invertī, inversum — turn something over or upside down; transitive. sē invertere — turn oneself over; the verb is also attested with a reflexive object.
  • cernuō, cernuāre — do a somersault; recorded by Morgan–Owens, including an Apuleius reference.
  • saltus cernuus; saltūs cernuī m. — somersault / acrobatic flip; singular nominative and genitive. Morgan–Owens lists the plural saltūs cernuī; the singular is inflected here from that expression.
  • Tabulam inverte. — Flip the plank over. Saltum cernuum fac. — Do a somersault.
  • These distinguish turning an object over from a bodily flip. They do not imply that a coin toss, switch operation, cartwheel and airborne backflip all have the same exact technical name.

Squeeze / squish / squash / crush

comprimō, comprimere; contundō, contundere

Ancient verbsSense distinctions
  • comprimō, comprimere, compressī, compressum — squeeze or press together, compress. Our practical choice for squishing something soft or squashing it down; the object supplies the soft/wet quality.
  • exprimō, exprimere, expressī, expressum — squeeze liquid out; also wring out the object containing it. Spongiam exprime. — Squeeze out the sponge. See also the food-preparation squeeze entry.
  • contundō, contundere, contudī, contūsum — pound, mash or crush by blows; Lewis & Short includes olives, roots and crushing/flattening injuries. The perfect has recorded quantity variation; contudī is left without a root-vowel macron here.
  • conterō, conterere, contrīvī, contrītum — grind or crush into small pieces; already covered in the cooking entry as well.
  • Lūtum comprime. — Squish / compress the mud. Spongiam nōlī comprimere. — Don’t squeeze the sponge.
  • Tamping and ramming: fistūcō, fistūcāre — ram down, tamp (Cato, Agr. 18.7 festūcātō; Vitruvius 7.1.1 fistūcātiōnibus); pīnsō, pīnsere — pound, beat; calcō, calcāre — tread or ram down (Pliny, NH 36.173 calcārī solum); īnferciō (īnfarciō), īnfercīre — pack or cram in (Pliny, NH 35.169 īnferciuntur, of rammed-earth walls).
  • English “squeeze,” “squish,” “squash” and “crush” overlap. These Latin choices distinguish compression, extraction, pounding and grinding; they are not four rigid one-to-one equivalents.
Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: comprimo · Lewis & Short: exprimo · Lewis & Short: contundo · Lewis & Short: contero · Lewis & Short: fistuco · Lewis & Short: pinso · Lewis & Short: calco · Lewis & Short: infarcio

Crash (verb) / crash (noun) / collision / crashing sound

collīdō, collīdere; collīsiō, collīsiōnis f.

Ancient wordsRecorded collision sense
  • collīdō, collīdere, collīsī, collīsum — dash or strike things together; transitive. To describe objects colliding, use the passive collīdī, with inter sē when appropriate.
  • collīsiō, collīsiōnis f. — collision; Morgan–Owens records the automobile application, citing Traupman. It also records collīsus, collīsūs m. with a Vatican Lexicon reference.
  • fragor, fragōris m. — crash or crashing sound; distinguishes the noise from the collision itself.
  • corruō, corruere, corruī — fall or collapse; useful when “crash” means coming down in a heap rather than hitting another object. Traupman also applies it to a computer crash; that is a separate modern extension.
  • Autoraedae inter sē collīduntur. — The cars crash into each other. Magnum fragōrem audīvī. — I heard a loud crash.
  • For toy cars the vehicle nouns have modern applications; the sentence is our composed description, not an ancient quotation.
Sources & evidence

currō, currere, cucurrī, cursum · festīnō, festīnāre

Ancient Latin
  • currō, currere, cucurrī, cursum — run.

Sprout / shoot

germen, germinis n.

Ancient Latin
  • germen, germinis n. — sprout, shoot, bud; germinō, germināre, germināvī, germinātum — sprout or put forth shoots.
  • pullus, pullī m. — young animal or young shoot; pullulō, pullulāre, pullulāvī, pullulātum — sprout or multiply.
  • Germen ē terrā oritur. — A sprout comes out of the earth.

Corn / maize

maizium, maiziī n.

Neo-LatinStem quantity uncertain
  • maizium, maiziī n. — maize; recorded in Morgan–Owens. This is an early modern Latin borrowing, not Classical vocabulary.
  • maiza, maizae f. — another recorded modern form; frūmentum Indicum — an attested descriptive alternative.
  • spīca, spīcae f. — ear of grain; extended to maize; grānum, grānī n. — grain or kernel; frūmentum, frūmentī n. — cereal grain collectively.
  • Scientific name: Zea mays. Botanical names are given in their conventional spelling.
  • The borrowing ultimately reflects Taíno through Spanish. The earlier exact “by 1493” claim is replaced by the broader, supportable early modern description.
  • Spīcam maiziī tenēs. — You’re holding an ear of corn.

The source establishes the word, not all its stem vowel lengths. Only the certain Latin inflectional quantity is marked in maiziī.

Sources & evidence

Morgan–Owens: Adumbratio

Husk / covering

involūcrum, involūcrī n.

Ancient wordsModern extension
  • involūcrum, involūcrī n. — wrapper, covering or envelope; folium, foliī n. — leaf.
  • glūma, glūmae f. — husk or glume of grain; palea, paleae f. — chaff or husk. Neither necessarily means the leafy outer covering of a maize cob.

Tomato

lycopersicum, lycopersicī n.

Neo-LatinLexicographic evidence
  • lycopersicum, lycopersicī n. — tomato; recorded in Morgan–Owens with botanical and modern lexical references.
  • tomāta, tomātae f. — an attested competing Neo-Latin form, cited there through Helfer.
  • Scientific plant name: Solanum lycopersicum.
  • tomātum is not preferred here. The earlier assertion that scholarship had specifically discredited it has been removed: a preference is not proof that a competing form is wrong.
  • Lycopersicum secō. — I’m cutting the tomato.
  • The tomāta family ultimately reflects Nahuatl through Spanish. lycopersicum is a learned botanical formation.

Cucumber

cucumis, cucumeris m.

Ancient Latin
  • cucumis, cucumeris m. — cucumber; ancient terminology need not map exactly onto a single modern species.
  • The alternate stem cucum- also occurs in ancient inflection; cucumer is a later or variant dictionary form, not required for ordinary use here.
  • cucumerārium, cucumerāriī n. — a cucumber bed.
  • Cucumerem secō. — I’m cutting the cucumber.
  • Cucumerem edis? — Are you eating the cucumber?
  • English cucumber ultimately comes from Latin through French; the deeper origin of the Latin word is uncertain.

Vitamin

vītamīnum, vītamīnī n.

Neo-LatinReading convention
  • vītamīnum, vītamīnī n. — vitamin; a modern lexical form. The feminine variant vitamina, vitaminae f. is also recorded by Morgan–Owens, without documented stem quantities.
  • vītamīna, vītamīnōrum n. pl. — vitamins, using the neuter form.
  • vītamīnicus, vītamīnica, vītamīnicum — pertaining to vitamins; a transparent derivative, not claimed here to be corpus-verified.
  • For a multivitamin preparation, praeparātum plūra vītamīna continēns is an explicit description; the previous unsupported claim for multivītamīnum has been withdrawn.
  • Hic cibus multa vītamīna continet. — This food contains many vitamins.
  • The international term was coined from “vita” and “amine”; it does not imply that all vitamins are amines.

The ī in vīta and the adopted international -amīn- reading give our convention vītamīnum; these are reconstructed Neo-Latin reading quantities, not attested Classical measurements.

Sources & evidence

Morgan–Owens: Adumbratio · Vitaminum: Calepinus Novus attribution

Ferment / fermentation

fermentum, fermentī n.

Ancient LatinScientific extension
  • fermentum, fermentī n. — leaven or ferment; fermentō, fermentāre, fermentāvī, fermentātum — cause to ferment or leaven. Intransitive fermentation can be expressed with the passive fermentārī.
  • fermentēscō, fermentēscere — begin to ferment or rise; ancient, attested in Pliny, not merely a later invention.
  • fermentātiō, fermentātiōnis f. — fermentation in scientific Latin. The ancient dictionary’s separately attested sense is “uniting”; its presence does not prove the modern biochemical meaning is Classical.
  • fervēscō, fervēscere — begin to boil or grow hot; not a precise synonym for microbial fermentation.
  • acēscō, acēscere, acuī — turn sour.
  • Lac fermentātur. — The milk is fermenting.

Yogurt / sour milk

jogurtum, jogurtī n.

Neo-LatinStem quantity uncertain
  • jogurtum, jogurtī n. — yogurt; recorded in Morgan–Owens. The formerly printed initial ō was not supported by the checked source and is no longer asserted.
  • lac acidum — sour milk; lac fermentātum — fermented milk; these are broader descriptions.
  • lac coāctum or lac concrētum — thickened or coagulated milk; descriptions of consistency.
  • coāgulum, coāgulī n. — rennet or coagulant; also a curdled mass in some contexts.
  • oxygala, oxygalae f. — ancient sour-milk preparation; oxygala, oxygalactis n. is also attested. Historical preparations and modern yogurt need not be identical.
  • Jogurtum edis? — Are you eating yogurt?

The loanword’s stem quantities remain undetermined here; the genitive ending -ī is certain.

Ancient wordsModern applications

  • holus, holeris n.; holera, holerum n. pl. — vegetable; vegetables or greens.

Strawberry / berries

frāgum, frāgī n.

Ancient wordModern application
  • frāgum, frāgī n.; frāga, frāgōrum n. pl. — strawberry; strawberries.
  • bacca, baccae f. — berry; a broad everyday word, not a strict modern botanical category. The spelling bāca, bācae f. is equally ancient (L&S).
  • Frāga lavā et in catīnum pōne. — Wash the strawberries and put them in the bowl.
  • Frāga congelāta — frozen strawberries.

Carrot / beetroot / pumpkin

carōta, carōtae f. · bēta, bētae f.

Ancient wordsModern species
  • carōta, carōtae f. — carrot; a Late Latin name. Classical pastināca, pastinācae f. has a broader, sometimes uncertain plant identification.
  • bēta, bētae f.; bēta rubra — beet; red beet or beetroot. Rādīx bētae specifies the root.
  • cucurbita, cucurbitae f. — gourd; extended here to pumpkin or squash.
  • pepō, pepōnis m. — Traupman’s alternative for pumpkin (p. 366). Classically pepō is a melon or large gourd (see the orchard entry); cucurbita remains our primary word.
  • Cucurbitam coctam adde. — Add the cooked pumpkin.
  • Carōtam rāde. — Grate the carrot.

The carrot name is ancient but not specifically claimed as Ciceronian. The pumpkin sense of cucurbita is a modern extension: the American species in these recipes differ from ancient gourds.

Neo-Latin

  • capsicum rubrum — red pepper.

Walnut / almond / peanut / nuts

jūglāns, jūglandis f.

Ancient wordsNeo-Latin peanut
  • nux, nucis f.; nucēs, nucum f. pl. — nut; nuts.
  • jūglāns, jūglandis f. — walnut; also the walnut tree (Lewis & Short: “a walnut; a walnut-tree”). The long ā in the nominative follows Traupman; it is not carried into the oblique stem. Varro, LL 5.102 derives the name from Jupiter’s acorn: ā Jove et glande jūglāns est appellāta. Pliny, NH 15.86 and 15.91: nucēs jūglandēs, with the green husk (calyx, calycis m.) and the woody shell (putāmen, putāminis n.).
  • amygdalum, amygdalī n.; amygdala, amygdalae f. — almond; both noun forms are documented.
  • arachis, arachidis f. — peanut; a modern botanical application, not an ancient American food name.
  • Nucēs omnīnō conterāmus. — Let’s grind the nuts completely.

Traupman supplies amygdalum and arachis; Morgan–Owens also records amygdala. The peanut loan’s stem quantities are not established here. Walnut shells and kernels belong to the fruit-parts entry.

Smoothie vocabulary: source audit and coverage

Pea / bean / lentil / chickpea / pulses

pīsum, pīsī n. · phasēlus, phasēlī m.

Ancient Latin
  • pīsum, pīsī n. — pea (Bulg. грах); Columella II 10, 4; Plīn. NH XVIII 123. Lewis & Short marks the ī long (late collateral pīsa, pīsae f.), and French pois continues the long vowel. pīsa viridia — green peas, our phrase for the shelled table vegetable.
  • phasēlus, phasēlī m. — the pod bean (Bulg. фасул, боб); Verg. G. I 227 (vīlemque phasēlum); Columella X 377. The modern green and kidney beans are an American species that inherited the ancient name (Phaseolus vulgaris, Linn.); Ep. VII uses phasēlī of Baba’s garden.
  • faba, fabae f. — the broad bean, the ancient staple bean (Bulg. бакла); Catō Agr. 35, 1; Plīn. NH XVIII 117. In the market stores of Ep. IV.
  • lēns, lentis f. — lentil (Bulg. леща); Plīn. NH XVIII 123; Catō writes the accusative lentim (Agr. 35). Also Ep. IV.
  • cicer, ciceris n. — chickpea (Bulg. нахут); Hor. S. I 6, 115 (ad porrī et ciceris … catīnum); the cēna rūstica of Ep. III.
  • siliqua, siliquae f. — pod (Bulg. шушулка); Varr. RR I 23, 3; Verg. G. I 74. The plural siliquae is pulse in general (Hor. Ep. II 1, 123).
  • legūmen, legūminis n. — any pulse or leguminous plant; Cic. ND II 156; already the Ep. III gloss for cicer.
  • Pīsa ē siliquīs exprimāmus. — Let’s pop the peas out of their pods.
  • Jūs ē phasēlīs coquitur. — Bean soup is cooking (Bulg. бобена чорба).

The bean words divide cleanly: faba is the ancient broad bean, phasēlus the pod bean whose name the American Phaseolus inherited, pīsum the pea. All quantities follow Lewis & Short.

Onion / leek / cabbage / sauerkraut / courgette / eggplant / potato / garlic / lettuce / radish / mushroom

caepa, caepae f. · brassica, brassicae f.

Ancient wordsModern species
  • caepa, caepae f. — onion (Bulg. лук); also spelled cēpa, with a neuter by-form caepe; the series’ spelling is caepa (Ep. VII).
  • porrum, porrī n. — leek (Bulg. праз); Plīn. NH XIX 108; Horace’s supper of leeks and chickpeas, S. I 6, 115.
  • brassica, brassicae f. — cabbage (Bulg. зеле); Catō Agr. 156, 1: brassica est quae omnibus holeribus antistat (ūsus: Ep. III, Culīna). brassica muriā condīta — sauerkraut (Bulg. кисело зеле), our phrase after Catō’s brined olives (Agr. 7, 4: conduntur … viridēs in muriā).
  • cucurbitula, cucurbitulae f. — courgette, zucchini (Bulg. тиквичка); the Culīna’s diminutive of cucurbita. The attested classical senses are a wild gourd and Celsus’s cupping-glass (Cels. II 11), so the vegetable sense is our extension.
  • melongēna, melongēnae f. — eggplant, aubergine (Bulg. патладжан); a medieval word from Arabic, kept in the botanical name Solanum melongena; Ep. VI (pitta cum melongēnīs).
  • pōmum terrestre; pōma terrestria — potato; potatoes (Bulg. картофи); Traupman 72, whose pulticula ex pōmīs terrestribus is mashed potatoes (ūsus: Culīna).
  • piperītis, piperītidis f. — the fresh pepper (Bulg. чушка); in Plīn. NH XX 174 a pepperwort; Traupman 71 applies it to the fresh Capsicum, and the series follows him (Epp. VI–VII). See the Red pepper entry for capsicum, and the pepper spice under piper.
  • Baba in hortō phasēlōs, caepās, cucumerēs colit. — Baba grows beans, onions and cucumbers in the garden (after Ep. VII).
  • ālium, āliī n. — garlic (Traupman 71; ā with Lewis & Short and de Vaan); lactūca, lactūcae f. — lettuce (71); rādīcula, rādīculae f. — radish (72); fungus, fungī m. — mushroom (72); cinara, cinarae f. — artichoke (70); caulis, caulis m. — cabbage stalk, kale.
  • in mēnsīs holitōriīs brassicae, porrī, carōtae, lactūcae, fungī — on the vegetable stalls, cabbages, leeks, carrots, lettuces, mushrooms (Fābula IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • epitonium ipse vertēbat brassicamque lavābat — he turned the tap on himself and washed the cabbage (Fābula III, Apud avum et aviam).

cf. Vulg. Num. 11, 5, where Israel remembers the cucumerēs, pepōnēs, porrī and cēpae of Egypt (cited at Lewis & Short, pepo). The potato, the eggplant and the sweet pepper are modern crops wearing borrowed names.

Cherry / peach / apricot / quince / melon / watermelon / chestnut

cerasum, cerasī n. · Persicum, Persicī n.

Ancient wordsModern species
  • cerasum, cerasī n. — cherry (Bulg. череша); Cels. II 24. The tree is cerasus, cerasī f., which Lucullus brought to Italy from Cerasūs in Pontus (Plīn. NH XV 102; Varr. RR I 39, 2) — a name-story that can be told as true.
  • Persicum, Persicī n. — peach (Bulg. праскова), the “Persian apple” (mālum Persicum); Plīn. NH XV 42; Mart. XIII 46. The tree is Persica, Persicae f.
  • Armeniacum, Armeniacī n. — apricot (Bulg. кайсия), the “Armenian apple” (mālum Armeniacum); Columella V 10, 19. The tree is Armeniaca (Plīn. NH XV 41).
  • cydōnium, cydōniī n.; pl. cydōnia — quince (Bulg. дюля), mālum cydōnium, the apple of Cydōnia in Crete; Varr. RR I 59; Plīn. NH XV 37; the Latinized spelling is cotōnea.
  • pepō, peponis m. — sweet melon (Bulg. пъпеш); Plīn. NH XIX 65; Vulg. Num. 11, 5. The Greek oblique stem (πέπων, -ονος) keeps its o short.
  • mēlopepō, mēlopeponis m. — the apple-shaped melon of Plīn. NH XIX 67; shortened late to mēlo, mēlōnis m. (Pallad. IV 9, 6), the ancestor of the modern melon-words.
  • citrullus, citrullī m. — watermelon (Bulg. диня); not ancient — a medieval word kept in the botanical name Citrullus lanatus. Stem quantities are conventional, not attested.
  • castanea, castaneae f. — chestnut (Bulg. кестен); Verg. Ecl. II 52 (castaneāsque nucēs); roasted as castaneae tostae in the Culīna, after the Conimbriga market of Ep. IV.
  • Cerasa Jūniō mātūrēscunt, Persica Augustō. — Cherries ripen in June, peaches in August.

All the orchard words but citrullus are ancient. Lewis & Short prints pepo, -ŏnis but mēlopepo, -ōnis; the shared Greek stem πέπων, -ονος settles both short, and the entries above follow the Greek.

Fog / mist / snow / rain / cloud / wind / frost / ice

nebula, nebulae f. · nix, nivis f.

Ancient Latin
  • nebula, nebulae f. — fog, mist (Traupman XV); nebulam dissipāre — disperse the fog.
  • nix, nivis f. — snow; ningit — it is snowing (Traupman 132); nivālis, nivāle — snowy (136).
  • pluit — it is raining; pluvia, pluviae f. — rain; nūbēs, nūbis f. — cloud; caelum cānum — a grey sky.
  • ventus, ventī m. — wind; ventus flat — the wind is blowing; Favōnius, Favōniī m. — the west wind (L&S).
  • gelū, gelūs n. — frost (Traupman 135); rigēre gelū — be stiff with frost; glaciēs, glaciēī f. — ice.
  • umbella, umbellae f. — sunshade, parasol (L&S); Fābula V compares the jellyfish to avus’s parachute: umbellae sunt, ave, sīcut tua in polō erat.
  • Tata, spectā! Nix est! Omnia nive tēcta sunt! — Dad, look! It’s snow! Everything is covered in snow! (Fābula II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • «Nōn est nix,» inquit, «sed nebula.» — “It isn’t snow,” he said, “it’s fog.” (Fābula II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • Mox sōl eam excitābit et abīre jubēbit — Soon the sun will wake it and send it away (Fābula II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • Pluet igitur; ita cornīx dīcit. — So it will rain; the crow says so. (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).

Seasons / months / when is it in season?

aestās, aestātis f. · hiems, hiemis f.

Ancient LatinComposed phrases
  • vēr, vēris n. — spring; aestās, aestātis f. — summer; autumnus, autumnī m. — autumn; hiems, hiemis f. — winter.
  • vēre, aestāte, autumnō, hieme — in spring, summer, autumn, winter (ablative of time).
  • mēnsis, mēnsis m. — month; mēnse Novembrī — in November; the month adjective alone also serves: Jūniō, Augustō, Septembrī, Octōbrī.
  • aestāte exeunte — at the end of summer; exeunte Novembrī — at the end of November.
  • Mōra nunc nōn sunt. — Cūr nōn sunt? Quandō erunt? — Aestāte exeunte, mēnse Augustō. Nunc November est. — There are no blackberries now. — Why not? When will there be? — At the end of summer, in August. Now it’s November. (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • Frāga Jūniō, in silvā. — Strawberries in June, in the woods. (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • Māla domī sunt, in cellā; autumnō enim leguntur. — The apples are at home, in the storeroom; they are picked in autumn. (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).

Mountain / hill / ridge / summit / valley / plain / slope / view

mōns, montis m. · collis, collis m.

Ancient Latin
  • mōns, montis m.; collis, collis m.; jugum, jugī n. — mountain; hill; ridge or pass (Traupman 204–206).
  • cacūmen, cacūminis n. — summit (Traupman 206).
  • vallis, vallis f.; convallis, convallis f. — valley; enclosed valley (L&S). campus, campī m. — plain (Traupman 205).
  • clīvus, clīvī m. — slope; clīvōsus, clīvōsa, clīvōsum — hilly, steep (Traupman 204, 206); arduus, ardua, arduum — steep (206); dēclīvis, dēclīve — sloping downhill; flexuōsus, flexuōsa, flexuōsum — winding (207).
  • prōspectus, prōspectūs m. — view (L&S).
  • Nix in monte est! Vidēsne? — There’s snow on the mountain! Do you see? (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • Inde prōspectus patēbat. — From there a view opened out. (Fābula II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • viā flexuōsā, angustā, arduā — by a winding, narrow, steep road (Fābula II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).

Sea / shore / river / stream / lake / spring / waterfall / cave / well

rīvus, rīvī m. · flūmen, flūminis n.

Ancient LatinComposed phrases
  • ōceanus, ōceanī m. — ocean; lītus, lītoris n. — shore, beach; ōra, ōrae f. — coast (Traupman 205); harēna, harēnae f. — sand; prōmunturium, prōmunturiī n. — cape, headland (L&S; Traupman 203 prints prōmontōrium). For mare see the Sailor and Waves entry.
  • flūmen, flūminis n. — river; rīpa, rīpae f. — bank; rīvus, rīvī m. — stream (Traupman 203); exārēscō, exārēscere, exāruī — dry up.
  • lacus, lacūs m. — lake (Traupman 204); stāgnum, stāgnī n. — pond (205).
  • fōns, fontis m. — spring, fountain; cataracta, cataractae f. — waterfall (L&S; Pliny).
  • spēlunca, spēluncae f. — cave, grotto (Traupman 203); puteus, puteī m. — well; cisterna, cisternae f. — cistern (L&S).
  • lapidēs per quōs trānsītur — stepping stones: the fābula’s description.
  • Rīvus, quī vēre strepit, siccus erat — The stream, which babbles in spring, was dry (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • Aestāte exeunte parum pluit, et aqua dēfēcit. — At the end of summer it hardly rained, and the water ran out. (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • «Tagus est,» inquit pater, «quī Lisbōnam praeterfluit et ibi in mare effunditur.» — “It’s the Tagus,” said Dad, “which flows past Lisbon and there pours into the sea.” (Fābula V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).

Forest trees: oak / beech / hornbeam / lime / ash / willow / hazel / pine

quercus, quercūs f. · tilia, tiliae f.

Ancient LatinIdentification notes
  • silva, silvae f. — forest, woods (Traupman 204); truncus, truncī m. — trunk; cortex, corticis m. — bark.
  • quercus, quercūs f. — oak; fāgus, fāgī f. — beech; carpinus, carpinī f. — hornbeam.
  • tilia, tiliae f. — lime, linden; fraxinus, fraxinī f. — ash; ulmus, ulmī f. — elm.
  • salix, salicis f. — willow; pōpulus, pōpulī f. — poplar, distinct from populus, people; pīnus, pīnī f. — pine.
  • corylus, corylī f. — hazel; cornus, cornī f. — cornelian cherry tree (Bulgarian дрян); spīnus, spīnī f. — blackthorn, sloe; jūglāns, jūglandis f. — walnut tree.
  • Tree names are mostly feminine, even in the second declension; rubus is masculine.
  • quercūs, tiliae, fraxinī, salicēs ad rīvum, jūglandēs, corylī, cornī — oaks, limes, ashes, willows by the stream, walnuts, hazels, cornelian cherries (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • Duae arborēs ibi stant etiam nunc, quercus et tilia, truncīs vīcīnīs, rāmīs jūnctīs. — Two trees stand there even now, an oak and a lime, their trunks side by side, their branches joined (Baucis and Philemon). (Fābula IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).

Fruit trees: apple tree / pear tree / fig tree / olive tree / vine

mālus, mālī f. · mālum, mālī n.

Ancient Latin
  • mālus, mālī f. — apple tree; mālum, mālī n. — apple (Traupman 70). Distinguish mālus, mālī m. — a ship’s mast, and malus — bad.
  • pirus, pirī f. — pear tree; prūnus, prūnī f. — plum tree; cerasus, cerasī f. — cherry tree.
  • fīcus, fīcī f. — fig tree; fourth-declension fīcus, fīcūs f. also occurs, and both are ancient.
  • olīva, olīvae f.; olea, oleae f. — olive tree and olive (L&S). arbor citrea — citron tree (L&S), usable for a lemon tree.
  • vītis, vītis f. — vine; pergula, pergulae f. — pergola, vine arbour; ūva in pergulā — grapes on the pergola.
  • Est in hortō mālus vetus, rāmīs humilibus et patulīs — In the garden there is an old apple tree with low, spreading branches (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • Spectā mē, Baba! Quam longē saluī! — Look at me, Baba! How far I jumped! (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • «Hīc olīva est,» inquit avia. «Ascende, sīmiole.» — “Here’s an olive tree,” said Grandma. “Climb up, little monkey.” (Fābula IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).

Moss / fern / ivy / grass / pine cone / rose / flower

muscus, muscī m. · nux pīnea

Ancient Latin
  • muscus, muscī m. — moss; filix, filicis f. — fern; hedera, hederae f. — ivy (L&S).
  • herba, herbae f. — grass, herb; grāmen, grāminis n. — grass, lawn; flōs, flōris m. — flower.
  • nux pīnea, nucis pīneae f. — pine cone (Plīn. NH XV 35; the fābulae’s word); also pīnea, pīneae f. (Col.). strobilus, strobilī m. is later (Digest) and stays out of the readers. pīneus, pīnea, pīneum — of pine.
  • rosa, rosae f. — rose; rosa canīna — dog rose, with red hips that are not eaten raw.
  • Ante portam Theodōrus nucem pīneam invēnit, magnam et sēmiapertam — In front of the gate Theo found a pine cone, big and half open (Fābula II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • Ubīque muscus est, in saxīs, in truncīs, in mūrīs; ubīque filicēs — Moss everywhere, on the rocks, on the trunks, on the walls; ferns everywhere (Fābula II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • Nōn sunt corna; rosae canīnae bācae sunt, quae crūdae nōn eduntur. — They aren’t cornelian cherries; they’re dog-rose hips, which aren’t eaten raw. (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).

Wild fruit and nuts on a walk: cornelian cherries / sloes / blackberries

cornum, cornī n. · prūnum silvestre

Ancient wordsIdentification notes
  • cornum, cornī n. — cornelian cherry, the fruit of cornus (Ov. corna; Bulgarian дрян).
  • prūnum silvestre — wild plum, sloe (Bulgarian трънки); Vergil speaks of spīnōs jam prūna ferentēs (Georg. IV 145).
  • mōrum, mōrī n. — blackberry by application; see the existing bramble entry (mōrum rubī).
  • bāca / bacca, -ae f. — berry; both spellings are ancient and both occur in the fābulae.

  • Prūna sunt, tata! Prūna invēnī! — Prūna quidem, sed spīnī — They’re plums, Dad! I found plums! — Plums indeed, but sloes (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • Nucēs Octōbrī. Quaere sub jūglande; fortasse ūna manet. — Nuts are in October. Look under the walnut tree; maybe one is left. (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • Ubi sunt mōra, tata? — Where are the blackberries, Dad? (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).

Birds: raven / crow / woodpecker / magpie / blackbird / sparrow / peacock / goose

corvus, corvī m. · cornīx, cornīcis f.

Ancient Latin
  • avis, avis f. — bird; volucris, volucris f. — winged creature, mainly poetic; rōstrum, rōstrī n. — beak; penna, pennae f.; plūma, plūmae f. — feather.
  • corvus, corvī m. — raven (Traupman 144); crōciō, crōcīre — croak (Plaut. Aul. 625; the fābula’s verb); crocitō, crocitāre — the frequentative (L&S); cornīx, cornīcis f. — crow (142).
  • pīcus, pīcī m. — woodpecker (Traupman 145); grāculus, grāculī m. — jackdaw; passer, passeris m. — sparrow; merula, merulae f. — blackbird; pīca, pīcae f. — magpie.
  • būteō, būteōnis m. — buzzard (Plin. NH X 21); noctua, noctuae f. — owl (Traupman 351).
  • pāvō, pāvōnis m. — peacock (Traupman 143); caudam explicāre — fan its tail. ānser, ānseris m. — goose.
  • corvōs, quī super agrōs crōciēbant, et cornīcēs, quārum ūna in fraxinō sedēns clāmābat — ravens croaking over the fields, and crows, one of which sat calling in an ash tree (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • Habetne pīcus malleum, tata? — Nōn malleum, sed rōstrum, quod illī prō malleō est. — Does the woodpecker have a hammer, Dad? — Not a hammer but a beak, which serves it as a hammer. (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • Ave, ecce avēs! Cūr caudās tam brevēs habent? — Grandpa, look, birds! Why do they have such short tails? (moulting peacocks) (Fābula V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).

Fish and seafood at the market: sardine / sea bass / bream / tuna / cod / shrimp / octopus / squid

piscis, piscis m. · sarda, sardae f.

Ancient wordsIdentification notes
  • piscis, piscis m. — fish; sarda, sardae f. — sardine (Traupman 73). Portuguese sarda is a mackerel.
  • lupus, lupī m. — sea bass, robalo (Hor., Mart.); aurāta, aurātae f. — gilthead bream, dourada (Col., Mart.); sargus, sargī m. — white bream, sargo (Ov., Plin.).
  • thynnus, thynnī m. — tuna (Traupman 145 prints thunnus); scomber, scombrī m. — mackerel (Plin.); trāchūrus, trāchūrī m. — horse mackerel (Plin.).
  • asellus, asellī m. — hake, cod (Plin. NH IX 61); asellus sale condītus et siccātus — salt cod, bacalhau; passer, passeris m. — flounder (Traupman 71).
  • squilla, squillae f. — shrimp (Traupman 73); ostrea, ostreae f. — oyster (72); locusta, locustae f. — lobster (71; L&S lŏcusta; de Vaan notes that lōc- and luc- are also found).
  • pōlypus, pōlypī m. — octopus, with long ō (Hor. Epod. 12, 5); lōlīgō, lōlīginis f. — squid; saepia, saepiae f. — cuttlefish (Plin. IX 83).
  • In mēnsīs piscātōriīs lupī jacēbant, aurātae, scombrī, pōlypī bracchiīs porrēctīs — On the fish stalls lay sea bass, gilthead bream, mackerel, octopuses with their arms spread out (Fābula IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Quid est in ventre piscis, tata? — What’s in the fish’s belly, Dad? (Fābula IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Hic piscis ānulum nōn habet. — This fish hasn’t got a ring. (Fābula IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).

Ancient fish names do not always map onto one modern species. The identifications follow the Fābula IV glosses, matched to Portuguese market names.

Aquarium: shark / ray / moray eel / starfish / sea urchin / seahorse / jellyfish / seaweed

squalus, squalī m. · raja, rajae f.

Ancient wordsModern senses
  • squalus, squalī m. — shark (Plin. NH IX 78); raja, rajae f. — ray (IX 78); cartilāgō, cartilāginis f. — cartilage.
  • mola, molae f. — sunfish: a modern sense (Mola mola); the Latin word means millstone. mūrēna, mūrēnae f. — moray eel (Plin. IX 76).
  • urtīca marīna — sea anemone (Plin. IX 146); stēlla marīna — starfish (IX 183); echīnus, echīnī m. — sea urchin (IX 100).
  • hippocampus, hippocampī m. — seahorse (Plin. XXXII 58); dracō marīnus — sea dragon, here the animal Phycodurus. Pliny’s dracō marīnus (IX 82) is a different fish.
  • pulmō marīnus — jellyfish (Plin. NH IX 154); medūsa — the modern name.
  • alga, algae f. — seaweed; concha, conchae f. — shell.
  • Mamma ossa habet, tata! — Habet. Raja piscis nōn habet. — Mummy has bones, Dad! — She does. A ray hasn’t got any. (Fābula V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
  • pulmōnēs marīnī pendēbant, vitreī, rotundī — jellyfish hung in the water, glassy and round (Fābula V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
  • hippocampī stābant ērēctī, caudīs algās amplexī — seahorses stood upright, their tails wrapped round the seaweed (Fābula V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).

Dolphin / whale / seal / otter / penguin / swim

delphīnus, delphīnī m. · sphēniscus, sphēniscī m.

Ancient wordsNeo-Latin
  • delphīnus, delphīnī m. — dolphin (Traupman 142); also delphīn, delphīnis m., accusative delphīna in Ovid.
  • bālaena, bālaenae f. — whale (Traupman 145; L&S bālaena).
  • phōca, phōcae f.; vitulus marīnus — seal (Plin. NH IX 19).
  • lutra, lutrae f. — otter; short u with de Vaan (from *udrā-), where L&S prints lūtra; lutra marīna — sea otter.
  • sphēniscus, sphēniscī m. — penguin, after the genus Spheniscus: the word of Fābula V (Neo-Latin); pinguīnus, pinguīnī m. is another Neo-Latin form.
  • natō, natāre, natāvī, natātum — swim; in dorsō natāre — swim on one’s back.
  • Avēs natant! Cūr nōn volant, tata? — In āëre nōn volant; in aquā volant. Sphēniscī vocantur — Birds swimming! Why don’t they fly, Dad? — They don’t fly in the air; they fly in the water. They’re called penguins (Fābula V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
  • Estne delphīnus in caelō, tata? Vidēre volō! — Is there a dolphin in the sky, Dad? I want to see it! (Fābula V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).

Orange / fig / hazelnut / prune / cranberry / ripe

mālum aurantium · fīcus, fīcūs f.

Ancient wordsNeo-Latin
  • mālum aurantium — orange (Traupman 72); aurantium, aurantiī n. — orange, as in Fābula III’s sūcus aurantiōrum; aurantius, aurantia, aurantium — orange-coloured. For the peach and the chestnut see the orchard entry.
  • fīcus, fīcūs f. — fig (the fruit); see the fruit-tree entry for the tree.
  • avellāna, avellānae f. — hazelnut (Traupman 71; Pliny’s nux Abellāna).
  • prūnum condītum — prune (Traupman 72).
  • oxycoccus, oxycoccī m. — cranberry (Morgan–Owens); descriptively baccae rubrae et acidae.
  • mātūrus, mātūra, mātūrum — ripe; amārus, amāra, amārum — bitter (Traupman 280); grandis, grande — big.
  • urceus sūcī aurantiōrum — a jug of orange juice (Fābula III, Apud avum et aviam).
  • Māla ad crustum emenda erant, nōn mollia sed dūra, nōn parva sed grandia — Apples had to be bought for the pie, not soft but firm, not small but big (Fābula IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).

Olives / olive oil / pick / basket

olīva, olīvae f. · oleum, oleī n.

Ancient Latin
  • olīva, olīvae f. — olive, tree and fruit; olea, oleae f. (L&S).
  • oleum, oleī n. — oil, olive oil (Traupman 72).
  • carpō, carpere, carpsī, carptum — pick; legō, legere, lēgī, lēctum — gather.
  • corbis, corbis f. — basket.
  • in sale condere — preserve in salt; olives become edible only after many days in salt.
  • «Olīvae sunt,» inquit avia. «Ex olīvīs oleum fit.» — “They’re olives,” said Grandma. “Oil is made from olives.” (Fābula III, Apud avum et aviam).
  • Quōmodo ex olīvīs oleum fit? — Premuntur, et oleum, quō coquō, exit. — How is oil made from olives? — They are pressed, and out comes the oil I cook with. (Fābula III, Apud avum et aviam).
  • Olīvās avia in corbem lēgit — Grandma gathered the olives into a basket (Fābula III, Apud avum et aviam).

Courier / delivery person

tabellārius, tabellāriī m.

Ancient wordsModern extension
  • tabellārius, tabellāriī m. — letter-carrier or courier; using it for a parcel delivery person is a modern application.
  • nūntius, nūntiī m. — messenger; cursor, cursōris m. — runner or courier; tabella, tabellae f. — writing tablet or letter.
  • nūntiō, nūntiāre, nūntiāvī, nūntiātum — announce or report.
  • Tabellārius adest. — The delivery person is here.
  • tabellārius is derived from tabella; cursor from currō. English nuncio, annunciation, cursor reflect these families.

Bus / coach

autoraeda longa

Neo-LatinLexicographic evidence
  • autoraeda longa — bus or coach; Morgan–Owens cites Albert, Helfer and Bacci. The noun is autoraeda, autoraedae f..
  • autocīnētum lāophoricum — a learned alternative; lāophorum, lāophorī n. — bus. The Greek-derived lāo- reflects “people,” and -cīnēt- “moving.”
  • autoraeda pūblica — public bus, also recorded in the modern lexicon.
  • Autoraedā longā īmus. — We’re going by bus.

Tram / streetcar

currus ēlectricus · currus trānsviārius

Neo-LatinLexicographic evidence
  • currus ēlectricus — tram (Traupman 218; Morgan–Owens): our preferred everyday term, used in Fābula V for the Lisbon eléctrico.
  • currus trānsviārius — tram; Morgan–Owens cites Palaestra Latina. currus, currūs m. — vehicle or carriage; trānsviārius, trānsviāria, trānsviārium — pertaining to a tramway.
  • pūblicus currus ēlectricus — another documented tram expression, cited there from the Lexicon Recentis Latinitatis.
  • currus tramviārius — a retained working alternative, with a borrowed tram- stem whose vowel length is not established here.
  • Currum trānsviārium exspectāmus. — We’re waiting for the tram.

Train / railway

trāmen, trāminis n.

Neo-LatinLexicographic evidence
  • trāmen, trāminis n. — train in modern Latin; trāmen ferriviārium — railway train.
  • ferrivia, ferriviae f. — railway; ferriviārius, ferriviāria, ferriviārium — pertaining to railways.
  • hamaxostichus, hamaxostichī m. — a competing learned Neo-Latin term for a train.
  • Morgan–Owens traces the lexical form trāmen to Charisius; the railway sense is modern. Related vocabulary: trahō, trahere, trāxī, tractum — draw or pull.

Bicycle / bicycle parts

  • birotārius, birotāria, birotārium — pertaining to bicycles; birotārius, birotāriī m. or birotāria, birotāriae f. — cyclist.

  • sessibulum, sessibulī n. — seat; sessibulum birotārium — bicycle saddle, recorded in LLH.
  • pedāle, pedālis n. — pedal; catēna, catēnae f. — chain; frēnum, frēnī n. — brake by modern extension; rota dentāta — toothed wheel or sprocket.
  • pneumaticum, pneumaticī n. — tyre in modern vocabulary; canthus, canthī m. — rim; luticipulum, luticipulī n. — mudguard, a modern formation.
  • compāgēs, compāgis f. — framework; applied to a bicycle frame; corpus birotāle — another modern lexical choice, explicitly recorded by LLH.
  • lanterna, lanternae f. — lamp; tintinnābulum, tintinnābulī n. — bell; antlia, antliae f. — pump.

Helmet / knee pads / elbow pads

galea birotāria

Ancient wordsModern extension
  • galea, galeae f. — helmet; galea birotāria — bicycle helmet, a transparent modern description.
  • genuāle, genuālis n. (plural genuālia) — knee covering or band; extended here to a protective knee pad.
  • cubital, cubitālis n. (plural cubitālia) — an elbow cushion in ancient Latin; extended here to an elbow pad.
  • chīrothēca, chīrothēcae f. — glove, a post-Classical word; chīrothēcae birotāriae — cycling gloves.
  • lōrum galeae — helmet strap.
  • Galeam indue. Genuālia et cubitālia indue. — Put on your helmet, knee pads and elbow pads.
  • Nunc birotam conscende. — Now get on your bicycle.

The specific protective-sports senses are labelled as semantic extensions; the earlier blanket “attested” tag has been removed.

Adventure / venture

ausum, ausī n. · adventūra, adventūrae f.

Ancient LatinMedieval LatinModern semantic extension
  • ausum, ausī n. — a daring attempt, venture, undertaking or enterprise; our preferred word for modern adventure when the emphasis is on something voluntarily and boldly undertaken.
  • adventūra, adventūrae f. — a medieval Latin word connected with what happens, chance, fortune, risk or venture; retained here as a secondary word for modern adventure by later semantic extension, especially through the Romance development of the word.
  • Novum ausum suscipiāmus. — Let’s undertake a new adventure.
  • Hodiē novum ausum quaerāmus. — Let’s seek a new adventure today.
  • Nova adventūra nōs exspectat. — A new adventure awaits us; a modern-style use, not presented as an ancient idiom.

The English word adventure ultimately belongs to the adventūra family, but its cheerful modern sense is later than the core medieval Latin meanings. For ordinary family speech, prefer ausum when an ancient word is wanted; use adventūra when the later European word-family itself is useful.

Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short / Logeion: ausum · Mittellateinisches Glossar: adventura · Medieval legal glossary: adventura / adventurare / adventurarius

Airport / aeroplane / runway / fly / take off / land

āëroportus, āëroportūs m. · āëroplanum, āëroplanī n.

Neo-LatinLexicographic evidence
  • āëroportus, āëroportūs m. — airport (Traupman 215); āëroplanum, āëroplanī n. — aeroplane (215); āëroplanō vehī — travel by plane (218).
  • āërodromus, āërodromī m. — runway (Traupman 218); a modern formation, narrower here than English aerodrome.
  • volō, volāre, volāvī, volātum — fly; volātus, volātūs m. — flight (Traupman 216).
  • sūrsum in āëra ascendere — take off (Traupman 218); ad terram dēscendere, deorsum appellere — land (217).
  • gubernātor, gubernātōris m. — pilot (Traupman 217); in ancient Latin a helmsman.
  • via āëria — air route; the fābula’s own descriptive phrase.
  • Āëroplanō vehēmur. — We’ll go by plane. (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Euax! Volāmus! Tata, volāmus! — Hooray! We’re flying! Dad, we’re flying! (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Rotae cum sonitū terram tetigērunt, et āëroplanum, sēnsim tardius currēns, tandem cōnstitit. — The wheels touched the ground with a thud, and the plane, running ever more slowly, at last stopped. (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).

The airport vocabulary follows Traupman, chapter XXIV. These are modern lexicographic formations on Greek and Latin roots, not ancient words; the diaeresis in āë- marks two separate vowels.

Gate / waiting room / departure / delay / layover / connection

aditus, aditūs m. · commorātiō, commorātiōnis f.

Ancient wordsNeo-Latin applications
  • aditus, aditūs m. — airport gate (Traupman 216); in ancient Latin an approach or entrance.
  • oecus praestōlātōrius — waiting room (Traupman 219); praestōlor, praestōlārī, praestōlātus sum — wait for (L&S).
  • abscēdō, abscēdere, abscessī, abscessum — depart; abscessus, abscessūs m. — departure (Traupman 216).
  • volātus dīlātus — delayed flight, from differō, differre, distulī, dīlātum (L&S); sērius — later; sērō — late.
  • commorātiō, commorātiōnis f. — layover, stopover (Traupman 217); conjūnctiō, conjūnctiōnis f. — connection (216).
  • āëroplana mūtāre — change planes (Traupman 215); ad āëroplanum sērius venīre — miss the plane, the fābula’s phrase (literally, reach it too late).
  • trānsitus, trānsitūs m. — transfer, transit: the fābula’s use (locūtiō nostra); L&S gives the general sense “a passing over”.
  • Ad aditum duodecimum oecus erat praestōlātōrius, sellīs multīs īnstrūctus — At gate twelve there was a waiting room with many seats (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Paulisper exspectandum est. — We’ll have to wait a little. (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Ibi āëroplana mūtābimus — There we’ll change planes (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Conjūnctiō bona est, neque tam brevis ut ad alterum āëroplanum sērius veniāmus, neque nimis longa. — It’s a good connection, not so short that we reach the second plane too late, and not too long. (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).

Security check / security officer / tray

scrūtātiō, scrūtātiōnis f.

Ancient wordsWorking formation
  • scrūtātiō, scrūtātiōnis f. — security check: the fābula’s descriptive term (locūtiō nostra), from scrūtor, scrūtārī, scrūtātus sum — search thoroughly (L&S). It is not a recorded Neo-Latin airport term.
  • custōs, custōdis m./f. — guard; here a security officer, feminine in Fābula VI.
  • cista, cistae f. — box or chest; applied in the fābula to the tray at the security check.
  • sarcinās excutere — search the bags (literally, shake them out; Fābula I); calceōs exuere — take off one’s shoes; see the existing shoe entry.
  • Ad scrūtātiōnem igitur ventum est, ubi custōdēs, nē quis rem perīculōsam in āëroplanum īnferat, omnium sarcinās excutiunt. — So they came to the security check, where the officers search everyone’s bags so that nobody takes anything dangerous onto the plane. (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Pēram in cistam posuit, lapidem, cum rogārētur, prōmpsit — He put his bag in the tray and, when asked, took out the stone (Fābula VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum).

Luggage / suitcase / backpack / luggage tag / luggage rack

sarcinae, sarcinārum f. pl. · vidulus, vidulī m.

Ancient wordsNeo-Latin applicationsWorking formation
  • sarcina, sarcinae f.; sarcinae, sarcinārum f. pl. — pack, bundle; luggage (Traupman 217). sarcina manuālis — hand luggage; Traupman 216 prints sarcinulae manuālēs.
  • vidulus, vidulī m. — suitcase (Traupman 218); in ancient Latin a travelling trunk (Plaut. Rud. 906 ff.). vidulus rotīs īnstrūctus — wheeled suitcase, the fābula’s description.

statiō ferriviāria · crepīdō, crepīdinis f.

Ancient wordsNeo-Latin applications
  • statiō ferriviāria — railway station (Traupman 219); statiō, statiōnis f. — station or stop.
  • crepīdō, crepīdinis f. — platform (Traupman 217); orbita, orbitae f. — track (219).
  • īnscendō, īnscendere, īnscendī, īnscēnsum; in trāmen īnscendere — board the train (Traupman 215); ē trāmine dēscendere — get off.
  • hōrārium trāminum — timetable (Traupman 218); sēdēs reservāta — reserved seat (218); currus, currūs m. — carriage (217).
  • trāmen commūne — local train (217); trāmen rapidissimum — express (216); trāmen dīrēctum — through train (219); trāmina mūtāre — change trains (215).
  • īnspector, īnspectōris m. — conductor (Traupman 216); chīliometrum, chīliometrī n. — kilometre (217).
  • In crepīdine exspectāvērunt — They waited on the platform (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • nec trāmen mūtāre opus est, nam rēctā Conimbricam it — and we needn’t change trains, for it goes straight to Coimbra (Fābula II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • Vēnit per ambulātiunculam īnspector tesserās poscēns — The conductor came down the aisle asking for tickets (Fābula II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).

Metro / underground / tunnel / tap the ticket

ferrivia subterrānea

Neo-LatinWorking formations
  • ferrivia subterrānea — underground, metro (Traupman 218); trāmen subterrāneum — metro train: the fābula’s descriptive phrase.
  • tesseram māchinae appōnere — tap the ticket on the reader: the fābula’s description (tesserae, quae māchinae appōnuntur ut porta aperiātur).
  • specus, specūs m. — tunnel; cave (Traupman 219, 203: Traupman prints only specus).
  • cunīculus, cunīculī m. — tunnel, underground passage: the ancient term. The same word means “rabbit” (see the animals entry).
  • columna, columnae f. — pillar; here the pole to hold on to.
  • Sub terrā currit trāmen, sub viīs, sub domibus — The train runs under the ground, under the streets, under the houses (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • ventus ē specū efflāvit, lūmina appāruērunt — a wind blew out of the tunnel, lights appeared (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Quot statiōnēs? — How many stops? (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Cum nūlla sēdēs vacua esset, stābant, et Theodōrus columnam tenēbat, ut virī solent. — As no seat was free, they stood, and Theo held the pole, as men do. (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).

Place names: Portugal / Lisbon / Coimbra / Sintra / Portuguese

Lūsitānia, Lūsitāniae f. · Lisbōna, Lisbōnae f.

Ancient namesPost-classical namesQuantity notes
  • Lūsitānia, Lūsitāniae f. — Portugal; the ancient name of the province (L&S). Lūsitānus, Lūsitāna, Lūsitānum — Portuguese; Lūsitānicē — in Portuguese, our adverb, formed like Latīnē.
  • Lisbōna, Lisbōnae f. — Lisbon, the form used in the fābulae (Braun & Hogenberg, Civitates orbis terrarum I, 1572, “vulgo Lisbona”); the ō follows Olisīpōn-. Olisīpō, Olisīpōnis m. — the ancient name (Pliny, NH 4.117; L&S Olisipo, with ī), for recognition.
  • Conimbrica, Conimbricae f. — Coimbra, a post-classical transfer of the name; Conimbriga, Conimbrigae f. — the Roman town nearby (Pliny 4.113 prints Conimbrica); Aeminium, Aeminiī n. — Roman Coimbra itself. Stem quantities are not established and are left unmarked.
  • Sintra, Sintrae f. — Sintra, the modern name declined in Latin (medieval Sintria; ancient Mōns Lūnae). Antanhol — the grandparents’ village, indeclinable.
  • Tagus, Tagī m. — the Tagus (L&S); Portus Cale — Porto; Alfama — indeclinable; statiō Orientālis — Gare do Oriente; Hortī Nātiōnum — Parque das Nações.
  • obrigado / obrigada — Portuguese “thank you”, from Latin obligātus, obligāta, “obliged”; the form agrees with the speaker.
  • Cities and small places take no preposition: Lisbōnam volābimus, Lisbōnae sumus, Sintrā (from Sintra); countries take one: in Lūsitāniam, in Lūsitāniā.
  • Ubi est Lūsitānia? Longēne abest? — Where is Portugal? Is it far away? (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Sintram īmus. — We’re going to Sintra. (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Scīsne, Theodōre, quid sit obrigado? Lūsitānī ita grātiās agunt. — Do you know, Theo, what obrigado is? That’s how the Portuguese say thank you. (Fābula IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).

The quantity of Lisbōna follows the fābulae and lexicon-notes-01; Conimbrica, Conimbriga and Serdica are left unmarked because their quantities are not established in the checked sources.

Serdica, Serdicae f. · Osoitsa, Osoitsae f.

Ancient namesModern names declined
  • Bulgaria, Bulgariae f. — Bulgaria; Bulgaricē — in Bulgarian.
  • Serdica, Serdicae f. — Sofia, the late-antique name, stem quantities left unmarked; Serdicae — in Sofia; Serdicēnsis — of Sofia.
  • Osoitsa, Osoitsae f. — Osoitsa, our village, first declension: Osoitsae (at), Osoitsam (to), Osoitsā (from); Osoitsēnsis — of Osoitsa.
  • Haemus, Haemī m. — the Balkan range, Stara planina (L&S); Rīla, Rīlae f. — Rila, declined in the fābulae; Vitosha — Vitosha, stem quantities unmarked.
  • Balī — Bali, indeclinable; hiemō, hiemāre, hiemāvī, hiemātum — spend the winter.
  • Baba, Babae f. — from Bulgarian баба, grandmother; the household name, declined in the fābulae (Babae, Babā).

Ancient namesNeo-Latin names
  • Eurōpa, Eurōpae f.; Polōnia, Polōniae f. — Poland; Cracōvia, Cracōviae f. — Kraków (Neo-Latin); Vistula, Vistulae f. — the Vistula (L&S).
  • Ītalia, Ītaliae f.; Bergomum, Bergomī n. — Bergamo (Plīn. NH III 124); āëroportus Bergomēnsis — Milan Bergamo airport (Fābula VI); Mediōlānum, Mediōlānī n. — Milan (L&S Mĕdĭōlānum).
  • Hispānia, Hispāniae f.; Gallia, Galliae f.; Alpēs, Alpium f. pl. — the Alps; Pȳrēnaeī, Pȳrēnaeōrum m. pl. — the Pyrenees.
  • mare Internum; mare Mediterrāneum — the Mediterranean (Traupman 205); mare Hadriāticum — the Adriatic (202); ōceanus Atlanticus — the Atlantic (205).
  • Corcȳra, Corcȳrae f. — Corfu (L&S).
  • America, Americae f.; Americānus, Americāna, Americānum — American; Brasilia, Brasiliae f. — Brazil, a later name; Brasiliānus — Brazilian; Anglicē — in English.
  • Tōta Eurōpa inter nōs et avum jacet. — All of Europe lies between us and Grandpa. (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Prīmum in septentriōnēs versus Cracōviam volābimus, quae urbs est Polōniae. — First we’ll fly north to Kraków, which is a city in Poland. (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Hīc Pȳrēnaeī montēs. — Here are the Pyrenees. (Fābula VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum).

Recorded vocabularyModern applicationsComposed descriptions
  • playground: ārea lūsōria; āreae lūsōriae f. — Traupman pp. 53, 361; Morgan–Owens also records campus lūsōrius and locus lūsōrius parvulōrum.
  • toy; toys: lūdibrium, lūdibriī n.; lūdibria, lūdibriōrum n. pl. — Traupman p. 396 explicitly gives toy. Ancient lūdibrium often means mockery/plaything; do not assume the neutral modern toy sense in every ancient occurrence. The second stem i has variable quantity in Lewis & Short; left unmarked here, following Traupman.
  • play; game: lūdō, lūdere, lūsī, lūsum; lūdus, lūdī m. — Ancient words. Lūdāmus! — Let’s play! Eāmus ad āream lūsōriam. — Let’s go to the playground.
  • equipment; toy version: īnstrūmentum, īnstrūmentī n.; lūsōrius, lūsōria, lūsōrium — Our productive toy descriptions below use lūsōrius; each full compound is labelled as composed unless independently recorded.
  • lūsōrium, lūsōriī n. — playground: our family’s own word (the Fābula VII gloss: ārea lūsōria (Traupman 53; vocābulum nostrum)), short for everyday use with Theo.
  • Eāmus ad lūsōrium, Baba, curriculō! — Let’s run to the playground, Baba! (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • lūsōrium autem, quod ante lūdum est, oscillīs et scālīs et tabulā dēclīvī īnstrūctum, semper patet — but the playground in front of the school, with its swings, ladders and slide, is always open (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).

Swing (transitive) / swing (intransitive) / playground swing

lībrō, lībrāre; oscillō, oscillāre

Ancient verbsSense distinctions
  • lībrō, lībrāre, lībrāvī, lībrātum — cause to swing, sway or brandish something; transitive. Lewis & Short II.B–C includes suspended movement and the swinging or brandishing of implements and weapons.
  • oscillō, oscillāre — swing oneself / swing to and fro; intransitive. Traupman explicitly records this on pp. 53 and 389; Lewis & Short cites Festus. No unverified perfect or supine is supplied.
  • oscillum, oscillī n. — swing apparatus; recorded by Traupman and Morgan–Owens for a playground swing. Verse locus: Vergil, G. 2.389 oscilla ex altā suspendunt mollia pīnū, which Lewis & Short cites both for the swing and for the little masks hung from trees.
  • impellō, impellere, impulī, impulsum — push or set in motion. Oscillum impelle. — Push the swing; our composed prompt for swinging someone on it.
  • Vīsne oscillāre? — Do you want to swing? Virgam lībrā. — Swing / brandish the rod. For gentle back-and-forth movement of a person, Tē hūc illūc movē. remains the descriptive prompt in our Monkey Tree Game.
  • pedēs porrigere / retrahere — stretch out / pull back the legs, to pump on a swing; our composed prompts.

Conversation, play & routines with Theo

Cum Theodōrō

43 entries

Totoro

Totorō, Totorōnis m.

Working formation
  • Totorō, Totorōnis m. — our playful third-declension adaptation of the Japanese name, not an established Latin form.
  • Genitive Totorōnis; dative Totorōnī; accusative Totorōnem; ablative Totorōne; vocative Totorō.
  • Theodōrus Totorōnem videt. — Theo sees Totoro.
  • Cum Totorōne per silvam ambulat. — He walks through the forest with Totoro.
  • Domus Totorōnis in silvā est. — Totoro’s house is in the forest.

The long final -ō in the nominative and vocative is part of our chosen Latin declension. The remaining name vowels follow our local reading convention.

Meow / cat’s cry

miau

Working formation
  • miau — a conversational imitation of a cat’s cry; no canonical Latin vowel quantities are assigned to the sound.
  • miaulō, miaulāre — our working verb “meow”; Latin inflectional endings are marked, but it is not labelled as established Neo-Latin. The earlier unsupported stem mī- is removed.
  • fēlēs, fēlis f. — cat; fēlēs clāmat — the cat cries or calls, using attested ancient vocabulary.
  • Fēlēs miaulat: miau, miau. — The cat meows: meow, meow.
  • The previous claim for an ancient Greek μιαῦ parallel has been removed because no ancient passage was supplied or verified.

Ancient Latin
  • baculum, baculī n. — stick or staff, useful for a stick picked up on a walk.
  • bacillum, bacillī n. — small staff, wand; the diminutive of baculum (Lewis & Short, citing Juvenal 3.28). Our reader series uses it for Theo’s stick. baculum is the walking staff; fustis, fustis m. is a club or cudgel.
  • virga, virgae f. — slender rod, switch or twig; rāmus, rāmī m. — branch or bough.
  • rāmulus, rāmulī m. or sūrculus, sūrculī m. — small branch, twig or shoot.
  • Baculum cape. — Pick up the stick.
  • Hic rāmus frāctus est. — This branch is broken.
  • Accusative plural: rāmōs. Both vowels are long; the lemma is rāmus.
  • pertica, perticae f. — longer pole; Morgan–Owens records the surveyor’s-rod sense. virga is the shorter/slender rod or wand; baculum the stick or staff. See also curtain rods in the household section.

petaurum, petaurī n.

Ancient wordModern extensionComposed phrases

petaurum, petaurī n. — a trampoline in our family vocabulary. The ancient word names an acrobatic apparatus; its precise ancient construction is debated. Leo Latinus uses it for the modern trampoline. This modern sense is not a claim that Romans had modern trampolines.

  • saliō, salīre — jump or leap.
  • saltus, saltūs m. — a jump or leap.
  • dēsultōrium, dēsultōriī n. — trampoline (Traupman 397); a secondary term beside petaurum.
  • pēs, pedis m. — foot; the ablative is pede, with short e.
  • In petaurō salī. — Jump on the trampoline.
  • Altius salī. — Jump higher.
  • Ūnō pede salī. — Jump on one foot. Ūnō agrees with masculine pede; this is an ablative of means.
  • Ambōbus pedibus salī. — Jump with both feet.
  • Iterum salī. — Jump again.
  • Dēsilī. — Jump down.

Monkey Tree Game / arm / branch / hanging / swinging

Sīmius et arbor

Ancient wordsFamily gameComposed phrases

Our Monkey Tree Game: Dad holds an arm horizontally, supports his fist with the other arm, and Theo jumps to grab the arm and swing from it. Sīmius et arbor means “The Monkey and the Tree” and works as a title without adding “game.” Lūdus sīmiī is the shorter explicit alternative, “The Monkey Game.” These are our game names, not attested ancient game titles.

  • sīmius, sīmiī m. — monkey or ape.
  • arbor, arboris f. — tree.
  • rāmus, rāmī m. — branch; in this game, Dad’s arm is the branch.
  • bracchium, bracchiī n. — arm.
  • pugnus, pugnī m. — fist. Short u: vowels before gn are short unless the stem is long (Bennett and Buck; Allen, Vox Latina). Lewis’s Elementary Latin Dictionary and de Vaan (s.v. pungō) print pūgnus, after Priscian’s rule.
  • lūdus, lūdī m. — game or play.
  • lūsus, lūsūs m. — playing, play or a game; its meanings overlap with lūdus.
  • prehendō, prehendere — grab or take hold of.
  • teneō, tenēre — hold.
  • pendeō, pendēre — hang; intransitive.
  • Ego arbor erō; tū sīmius eris. — I’ll be the tree; you’ll be the monkey.
  • Bracchium meum prehende. — Grab my arm.
  • Salī et bracchium meum prehende. — Jump and grab my arm.
  • Firmē tenē. — Hold tight.
  • Ē rāmō pendē. — Hang from the branch.
  • Tē hūc illūc movē. — Move yourself back and forth; a simple prompt for swinging.

Sailor and Waves / duvet sea game / bedtime / balance / falling / tumbling

Nauta et undae

Ancient wordsFamily gameComposed phrases

Our bedtime sea game: Theo stands on the duvet while Dad holds a corner or side and moves it to make waves; Theo jumps, falls and tumbles. Nauta et undae means “The Sailor and the Waves.” The title is our own. Strāgulum is a broad bed-covering word, used here for the duvet without specifying its filling.

  • strāgulum, strāgulī n. — bed covering; our practical word for the duvet in this game.
  • angulus, angulī m. — corner.
  • latus, lateris n. — side, with short a; distinguish lātus, “broad.”
  • mare, maris n. — sea.
  • unda, undae f. — wave.
  • nauta, nautae m. — sailor.
  • nāvis, nāvis f. — ship or boat.
  • aequilībrium, aequilībriī n. — balance or equilibrium; applied here to keeping one’s balance.
  • genū, genūs n.; plural genua — knee; knees. The u in the plural genua is short: no macron.
  • moveō, movēre — move.
  • tollō, tollere — lift.
  • dēmittō, dēmittere — lower or let down.
  • agitō, agitāre — move about, shake.
  • undō, undāre — billow, undulate; intransitive in our phrases. Ancient usage includes a billowing cloak.
  • flectō, flectere — bend.
  • jactō, jactāre — toss about.
  • cadō, cadere — fall.
  • volūtō, volūtāre — roll or tumble about; use tē for “roll yourself.”
  • stō, stāre — stand.
  • dēsinō, dēsinere — stop or cease.
  • Tū nauta es; hoc est mare. — You’re the sailor; this is the sea.
  • In strāgulō stā. — Stand on the duvet.
  • Strāgulī angulum teneō. — I’m holding a corner of the duvet.
  • Strāgulī latus teneō. — I’m holding a side of the duvet.
  • Strāgulum tollō et dēmittō. — I lift and lower the duvet.
  • Strāgulum moveō ut undet. — I move the duvet so that it billows.
  • Strāgulum undat. — The duvet is billowing.
  • Ecce unda magna. — Here comes a big wave.
  • Vīs undās magnās an parvās? — Do you want big waves or little waves?
  • Undās fac. — Make waves.
  • Genua flecte. — Bend your knees. All three vowels in genua are short in the ordinary three-syllable form.
  • Aequilībrium servā. — Keep your balance.
  • Undīs jactāris. — You’re being tossed by the waves.
  • Cecidistī. — You fell.
  • Cecidī. — I fell.
  • Tē volūtā. — Roll around.
  • Iterum stā. — Stand up again.
  • Dēsine. — Stop.
  • Iterum. — Again.

The game’s imagery and example sentences are composed for Theo. Undāre describes the duvet billowing; to make it billow, we move it (moveō, agitō). We do not use transitive strāgulum undō, which would suggest flooding the duvet.

Mission / assigned task / quest / search

mūnus, mūneris n.; expedītiō, expedītiōnis f.

Ancient sensesPlaytime applications
  • mūnus, mūneris n. — task, duty or function; our choice for a playtime “mission.” mandātum, mandātī n. — commission, instruction or something entrusted to someone.
  • opus, operis n. — a work or job, including one a child sets himself; better than mūnus, which is a duty laid on someone. Opus perfēcistī! — You’ve finished the job!
  • expedītiō, expedītiōnis f. — expedition or campaign in ancient usage; our contextual application to an adventurous playtime quest. It is not presented as a verified fixed translation of a modern fantasy-game quest.
  • investīgātiō, investīgātiōnis f. — search or investigation; use for the searching activity itself. For an adventure as a daring undertaking, the existing adventure entry prefers ausum, ausī n..
  • Hoc est mūnus tuum: uncum reperī. — Here’s your mission: find the hook. Eāmus thēsaurum quaesītum! — Let’s go look for treasure! The latter uses the supine of purpose after a verb of motion.
  • These are contextual choices for conversation with Theo. The adventure and search senses need not be expressed by the same noun.

Macte virtūte!

Classical idiomsQuotations

Walk / fork in the road / which way? / this way, that way / pocket full of stones

ambulātiō, ambulātiōnis f. · trivium, triviī n.

Ancient Latin

Greetings: goodbye / have a good flight / welcome / I’m glad you’re back

Valē! · Salvum tē advēnisse gaudeō.

Classical quotationsFamily phrases
  • Valē! Valēte! — Goodbye!; Bene volāte! — Have a good flight!
  • Ī, bene ambulā. — Off you go, safe journey (Plaut. Asin. 108, where the manuscripts spell the imperative ei; also Traupman 212).
  • Redī cito. — Jam ego hīc erō. — Come back soon. — I’ll be back in no time. The first is said by the one who stays, the second by the one who leaves (Plaut. Men. 225).
  • Salvum tē advēnisse gaudeō. — I’m glad you’ve arrived safely, said by the one who waits (Ter. Phorm. 286); to a woman salvam, to several salvōs vōs.
  • Mea māter, salvē. — Gaudeō vēnisse salvum. — the son arriving, the mother waiting (Ter. Hec. 353). This parallels Bulgarian Добре заварил / Добре дошъл.
  • Ō pater, pater mī, salvē. — Salvē multum, gnāte mī. (Plaut. Trin. 1180); Vēnistī! Ō mihi nūntiī beātī! (Catull. 9, 5).
  • «Valēte,» inquit, «bene volāte! Theodōre, patrī pārē, et aviae meīs verbīs salūtem dīc.» — “Goodbye,” she said, “have a good flight! Theo, do what Dad says, and give Grandma my love.” (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • bene ambulā et redambulā — safe journey there and back (Plaut. Capt. 900; quoted in Fābula VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum).

On the way: where are we going? / why? / not yet / too early / it’s getting dark / not far now

Quō īmus? — Ad avum īmus.

Family phrasesClassical quotations
  • Quō īmus? — Cūr? — Where are we going? — Why? Theo’s own travel questions in the fābulae. Jam advēnimus? — Nōndum. — Are we there yet? — Not yet (composed; Theo never asks it).
  • Nimis paene māne est. — It’s far too early (Plaut. Persa 114); Māne quod tū occēperis negōtium agere, id tōtum prōcēdit diem. — what you start in the morning goes well all day (114–115).
  • Quid stās? quid cessās? — Why are you standing there? Why the delay? (Ter. And. 979).
  • Brevis est via. — It won’t be long (Verg. Ecl. 9, 23, via Ranieri).
  • Jam advesperāscit. — It’s getting dark already (Ter. And. 581); vesperāscit — evening is coming.
  • Fīat lūx. — Let there be light (Gen. 1:3), when the light goes on.
  • Quō īmus, tata? — Ad avum īmus. — Where are we going, Dad? — We’re going to Grandpa’s. (Fābula II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • Quandō rūrsus volābimus? — Mox. Nōndum dīmidium itineris cōnfēcimus. — When will we fly again? — Soon. We haven’t done half the journey yet. (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Nimis paene māne est. — It’s almost too early. (Plaut. Persa 114; quoted in Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • surge et ambulā — get up and walk: Dad, lifting the sleeping boy out of bed (Mt 9, 5, in jest; quoted in Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).

Safety and instructions: careful, don’t fall / don’t touch / mind your fingers / come here

Cavē nē cadās; astā.

Family phrasesClassical quotations
  • Cavē nē cadās; astā. — Careful you don’t fall; stand still (Plaut. Most. 324). In Fābula VII Theo sings it himself.
  • Nōlī tangere.; Nē tangās. — Don’t touch. Prohibitions take nōlī + infinitive, nē + perfect subjunctive, or in everyday speech nē + present subjunctive (Traupman 33, as cited).
  • Cavē digitōs. — Mind your fingers; Manum alteram procul. — Keep your other hand away.
  • Ad pinnās, nōn ad marginem. — Stay by the wall, not by the edge.
  • Hoc facitō; hoc fugitō. — Do this; avoid that (Ter. Ad. 417).
  • Ōcius hūc ades! — Come here, quickly! (Verg. Ecl. 7, 8–9, via Ranieri).
  • Tacē. — Be quiet; Tacē, occultēmus lūmen et vōcem. — Licet. — Hush, let’s hide the light and our voices. — All right (Plaut. Curc. 95), for a game in the dark.
  • Ostende hūc manūs. — Em tibi, ostendī, eccās. — Show me your hands. — There you are, look (Plaut. Aul. 640–641); Satis est; terge. — That’s enough; dry them.
  • Nōlī tangere, Theodōre; calidissima sunt. — Don’t touch, Theo; they’re very hot. (Fābula IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Digitōs laevae ā cultellō procul habē; cavē nē digitum secēs. — Keep the fingers of your left hand away from the knife; mind you don’t cut a finger. (Fābula IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Pater «Cavē nē cadās,» inquit; quod puer, dum scandit, ipse sibi cantat. — Dad said “Careful you don’t fall”; and the boy sings it to himself as he climbs. (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • Cavē nē cadās, astā. — Careful you don’t fall; stand still. (Plaut. Most. 324; also in Fābula II).

Days of the week

diēs Lūnae · diēs Sōlis

Neo-LatinLexicographic evidence
  • diēs Lūnae — Monday; diēs Mārtis — Tuesday; diēs Mercuriī — Wednesday (not in the fābulae; added to complete the week).

  • Diēs Sōlis prīmus post reditum illūxit — Sunday dawned, the first day after their return (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).

Telling the time: quarter past / half past / afternoon / later / ago

hōra, hōrae f. · quadrāns, quadrantis m.

Ancient wordsModern application
  • hōrā decimā et quadrante — at 10:15 (Traupman X); hōrā nōnā et dīmidiā — at 9:30.
  • post merīdiem — in the afternoon, p.m.; ante merīdiem — a.m.
  • dōdrāns hōrae — three quarters of an hour (dōdrāns, dōdrantis m.; Cic., Plin.).
  • vesperī — in the evening; sērō — late; sērius — later.
  • abhinc — ago; post quīnque diēs — in five days’ time.
  • Nōbīs enim multō māne surgendum: āëroplanum hōrā decimā et quadrante abscēdet — For we must get up very early: the plane leaves at a quarter past ten (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • abhinc plūs mīlle annōs in summō monte castellum aedificāvērunt — more than a thousand years ago they built a castle on the top of the mountain (Fābula II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • Mīlle annōs, tata? Mīlle multī sunt! — A thousand years, Dad? A thousand is a lot! (Fābula II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).

For minutes the lexicon uses neuter minūtum, minūtī n. (measures entry); feminine minūta, minūtae f. (Traupman 87) is also current.

numerō, numerāre · semel, bis, ter

Ancient Latin
  • numerō, numerāre, numerāvī, numerātum — count.
  • ūnus, duo, trēs, quattuor, quīnque, sex — the first numbers, as Theo counts the apples.
