Saying grace / giving thanks / Thanksgiving Day / fold your hands

grātiās agere · Diēs Grātulātiōnis

Ancient LatinNeo-LatinFamily phrases
  • grātiās agere (+ dative of the person; prō + ablative of the thing) — give thanks, say grace (Traupman 393).
  • Diēs Grātulātiōnis — Thanksgiving Day (Traupman 393; Vicipaedia); Fēlīcem Diem Grātulātiōnis! (393). Classical grātulātiō is a public thanksgiving (Cic.). This is preferred to the periphrastic diēs grātiārum āctiōnis (Morgan–Owens).
  • manūs jungere — fold one’s hands; oculōs claudere — close one’s eyes; caput inclīnāre — bow one’s head.
  • Ōrātiō Dominica — the Lord’s Prayer; Āmēn.
  • Cōnfitēminī Dominō, quoniam bonus: quoniam in aeternum misericordia ejus. (Ps. 135 [136], 1) — said responsively, Dad the first half-verse and Theo the second.
  • grātiās agere is thanking in words; grātiam referre is repaying in deed (Cic. Off. I 47).
  • Pater caelestis, grātiās tibi agimus prō hōc cibō, prō hāc domō — Heavenly Father, we thank you for this food, for this home (Fābula IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Ego grātiās agō. — I say thank you. (Fābula IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Quia haec omnia dōna sunt. — Because all these things are gifts. (Fābula IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).

Coffee / make coffee

coffea, coffeae f.

Neo-LatinStem quantity uncertain
  • coffea, coffeae f. — coffee; an attested modern noun, recorded with botanical and literary references in Morgan–Owens.
  • cafēa, cafēae f. or caffēa, caffēae f. — recorded alternatives; the draft explicitly marks their ē. The unmarked spelling coffea there does not establish an equally certain stem quantity.
  • caffēa, caffēae f. — our preferred alternative in speech; caffea — Traupman’s spelling (p. 70), printed without a marked ē. Both are recorded alternatives; the headword coffea stands.
  • pōtiō Arabica — coffee, a descriptive phrase recorded in the Lexicon Recentis Latinitatis and noted in the Fābula I gloss on caffea.
  • coffeam parāre — prepare coffee; coffeam coquere — brew it by heating.
  • Coffeam parō. — I’m making coffee.
  • Vīsne ut coffeam parem? — Shall I make coffee?

For coffea, the stem length is left uncertain instead of claiming that every plain vowel is historically short.

Peanut butter / almond butter / walnut butter / plant milk / soy / coconut

būtȳrum ex arachidibus · lac sojae

Recorded Neo-LatinWorking descriptions
  • būtȳrum, būtȳrī n.; būtȳrum ex arachidibus — butter; peanut butter. The latter is explicitly recorded by Traupman.

Lac, lactis n. is extended from animal milk to plant drinks. These are names for the foods, not assertions that all products have equivalent nutrition. Soja has no stem length claimed beyond the checked evidence.

būtȳrum is written with long ȳ, from βούτῡρον (βοῦς + τῡρός); Lewis & Short also records the short-y form būtyrum.

Smoothie / juice / pulp / flavour / thick / thin

pōtiō, pōtiōnis f.

Ancient wordsWorking description
  • pōtiō, pōtiōnis f. — drink; our short contextual word for a smoothie.
  • pōtiō ex pōmīs holeribusque contrītīs — a drink made from blended fruit and vegetables; our explicit description, not a claimed standard Neo-Latin headword.
  • sūcus, sūcī m. — juice; not an exact synonym for a whole-food smoothie.
  • pulpa, pulpae f. — flesh or pulp; fruit-pulp use is documented in post-classical sources.
  • sapor, sapōris m.; odor, odōris m.; spūma, spūmae f. — taste or flavour; smell or aroma; foam.
  • Pōtiō nimis crassa est. Aquam addāmus. — The smoothie is too thick. Let’s add water.
  • Haec pōtiō tenuis est; illa dulcis est. — This smoothie is thin; that one is sweet.
  • liquor, liquōris m. — liquid.

The drink label and complete smoothie phrase are our working descriptions. Crassus/tenuis describe consistency; dulcis, acidus and amārus describe sweetness, sourness and bitterness.

The noun is pōtiō with long ō (L&S pōtio; cf. pōtus, pōtāre); the earlier short-o spelling was corrected on 23 October 2026.

culter coquīnāris · incīsōrium, incīsōriī n.

Ancient wordsMedieval extensionWorking peeler phrase
  • culter, cultrī m.; culter coquīnāris — knife; kitchen knife, recorded in both modern references.

Tablespoon / teaspoon / handful / pinch / portion / gram / millilitre / seconds

cochlear majus · cochlear minus

Modern measuresQuantity notes
  • cochlear, cochleāris n.; cochlear majus; cochlear minus — spoon or spoonful; tablespoon; teaspoon. The larger/smaller-spoon expressions are recorded in Morgan–Owens.
  • manipulus, manipulī m. — handful, especially of leaves or herbs.
  • paulum, paulī n. — a little; paulum cinnamōmī is our easy way to say “a pinch of cinnamon,” without implying an exact measure.
  • pars, partis f.; portiō, portiōnis f.; dimidium, dimidiī n. — part; portion; half.
  • gramma, grammatis n.; millilitrum, millilitrī n. — gram; millilitre, as modern metric units in pharmaceutical Latin.
  • minūtum, minūtī n.; minūtum secundum — minute; second, in modern time measurement.
  • Duo cochleāria adde. Dimidium pirum mihi dā. — Add two spoonfuls. Give me half a pear.
  • mētior, mētīrī — measure; pendō, pendere — weigh. Aquam mētīre; nucēs pende. — Measure the water; weigh the nuts.
  • index, indicis m. rērum emendārum — shopping list; our descriptive phrase. mēnsūra, mēnsūrae f.; pondus, ponderis n. — measure; weight.

These recipes use modern measuring spoons (tablespoon 15 ml; teaspoon 5 ml), not the capacity of an ancient cochlear. Metric forms are documented in pharmaceutical Latin; unverified millilitrum stem quantities are left unmarked. See the source audit for the technical usage reference.

minūtum, minūtī n. is the headword here; feminine minūta, minūtae f. (Traupman 87) is also current.

  • cortex, corticis m.; cutis, cutis f. — rind or peel; skin. Cortex is also sometimes feminine in ancient usage.

  • putāmen, putāminis n. — shell or husk; especially a walnut shell here.

The apple-core description and specific kitchen uses are composed for clarity. Fruit stones, nut kernels and seeds are related objects, not automatic synonyms in every context.

  • dēcorticō, dēcorticāre — strip the bark or peel; applied here to fruit. No unattested perfect is supplied.

  • Pōma lavā. Urceum ēlue. — Wash the fruit. Rinse the jug.
  • Corticem banānae aufer. — Remove the banana peel.
  • Partem mediam mālī cum sēminibus exime. — Remove the middle of the apple with the seeds; core the apple.
  • Capsicī sēmina exime. — Remove the pepper’s seeds; deseed the pepper.

“Core” and “deseed” are expressed with ordinary objects and verbs rather than unsupported one-word technical coinages. The prompts are newly composed, not quotations from the dictionaries.

John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 72 (cutem resecāre), as cited in Fābula IV.

Cut / chop / dice / slice / halve

secō, secāre · concīdō, concīdere

Ancient verbsDescriptive precision
  • secō, secāre, secuī, sectum — cut.
  • concīdō, concīdere, concīdī, concīsum — cut up or chop; distinguish concidō with short i, “fall down.”
  • minuō, minuere; comminuō, comminuere — make smaller; break or reduce to little pieces.
  • in frūstula secāre; minūtātim concīdere — cut into small pieces; chop finely.
  • in frūstula cubica secāre — dice; our descriptive phrase, literally cut into small cube-shaped pieces.
  • in segmenta secāre; in duās partēs secāre — slice; cut into two parts or halve.
  • Ego secābō; tū frūstula in catīnum pōne. — I’ll cut; you put the pieces in the bowl.
  • resecō, resecāre — cut back or trim. Partēs dūrās resecā. — Trim off the tough parts.

The verbs are ancient. Exact dice size, kitchen technique and modern cube-shaped-piece phrasing are our descriptions. We do not present every English cooking verb as requiring its own distinct Latin verb.

Smoothie vocabulary: source audit and coverage

Grate / grind / crush / blend / mix / stir

rādō, rādere · conterō, conterere · misceō, miscēre

Ancient verbsModern blender use
  • rādō, rādere, rāsī, rāsum — scrape; applied to grating with a rādula.
  • terō, terere, trīvī, trītum; conterō, conterere, contrīvī, contrītum — grind or rub down; grind or crush thoroughly.
  • misceō, miscēre, miscuī, mixtum — mix or blend; mixing alone need not imply that solid pieces have been ground smooth.
  • agitō, agitāre — stir or agitate in an appropriate cooking context.
  • Carōtam rādulā rāde. — Grate the carrot with the grater.
  • Pōma māchinā concīsōriā conterāmus. — Let’s blend the fruit with the blender.
  • Omnia misce et tere, dōnec frūstula nūlla supersint. — Mix and blend everything until no little pieces remain.
  • cōlō, cōlāre — strain or filter. Pulpam servā; pōtiōnem nōlī cōlāre. — Keep the pulp; don’t strain the smoothie.
  • For conterere contrasted with pounding, compression and squishing, see squeeze / squish / squash / crush.

Using these ancient verbs for an electric blender is a modern application. Conterere describes breaking the solids down; miscēre describes combining ingredients. The apparatus phrase supplies the modern context.

Pour / add / squeeze / scoop / transfer / fill

īnfūndō, īnfundere · addō, addere

Ancient verbsComposed prompts
  • īnfundō, īnfundere; fundō, fundere — pour into; pour. The macron convention in īnf- follows the existing lexicon; the root vowel in fundō remains short.
  • addō, addere; pōnō, pōnere — add; put or place.
  • exprimō, exprimere; premō, premere — squeeze out; press.
  • eximō, eximere; trānsferō, trānsferre; impleō, implēre — take or scoop out; transfer; fill.
  • Sūcum citreī exprime. — Squeeze out the lemon juice.
  • Pulpam avacātī cochleārī exime. — Scoop out the avocado flesh with a spoon.
  • Pōtiōnem in pōcula īnfunde. Nōlī nimis implēre. — Pour the smoothie into the glasses. Don’t fill them too much.
  • Spongiam exprime. — Squeeze out the sponge; the same ancient verb works beyond food. For compression without extracting liquid, see comprimere.

Ordinary Latin verbs cover the actions. Scooping is expressed with eximere plus the spoon as an instrument; no separate unsupported kitchen neologism is required.

The modern kitchen contexts do not make these verbs inventions. Phrases about steam cooking and thawing are descriptive applications. Consult food-package instructions separately; this is vocabulary, not a cooking-safety specification.

Smoothie vocabulary: source audit and coverage

Nutrition / protein / fibre / fat / calcium / sugar / vitamins

nūtrītiō, nūtrītiōnis f.

Technical Neo-LatinAncient roots
  • nūtrītiō, nūtrītiōnis f.; pars nūtriēns, partis nūtrientis f. — nutrition or nourishing; nutrient, with a descriptive part-that-nourishes phrase recorded by Morgan–Owens.
  • proteīnum, proteīnī n. — protein; recorded in Morgan–Owens’s Silva through Helfer/Heyse. The checked entry marks ī but does not establish every stem quantity.
  • fībra, fībrae f.; fībrae alimentāriae — fibre; dietary fibre, our modern technical description. Classical fibra by itself does not specifically mean dietary fibre.
  • adeps, adipis m. or f. — fat; applied in a nutritional context.
  • calcium, calciī n.; saccharum, saccharī n. — calcium; sugar. The chemical-element sense is modern; saccharum is ancient.
  • vītamīnum, vītamīnī n.; vītamīna D et B12 — vitamin; vitamins D and B12. The existing vitamin entry explains the adopted reading convention.
  • vīs, vīs f.; vīrēs, vīrium f. pl. — strength or power; energy in a broad everyday sense, not a precise unit of food energy.

These names let us discuss the guide without turning modern nutritional categories into supposedly Classical concepts. Chemical and loanword quantities remain limited to the checked evidence.

Smoothie vocabulary: source audit and coverage

White cheese / yellow cheese / banitsa / tarator / lyutenitsa

cāseus albus · placenta, placentae f.

Ancient wordsModern descriptions
  • cāseus albus (muriā condītus) — sirene, the Bulgarian white brined cheese (Bulg. сирене); our description, brined on the model of Catō’s green olives (Agr. 7, 4: conduntur … viridēs in muriā).
  • cāseus flāvus — kashkaval, the firm yellow cheese (Bulg. кашкавал); our description.
  • placenta, placentae f. — Catō’s layered cake of dough sheets (tracta) and cheese, built sheet by sheet (Agr. 76, ūsus: Culīna; Hor. Ep. I 10, 11) — the nearest ancient thing to banitsa (Bulg. баница). placenta cāseō farta — a cheese-filled banitsa.
  • jūs frīgidum ex jogurtō cucumereque — tarator, the cold yogurt-and-cucumber soup (Bulg. таратор); our description. For the yogurt loan see the jogurtum entry.
  • condīmentum ex piperītidibus trītīs — lyutenitsa, the roasted-pepper relish (Bulg. лютеница); our description.
  • Māne placentam calidam ēmimus. — In the morning we bought a warm banitsa.

placenta is attested and genuinely layered, so it carries the banitsa idea honestly; the Romanian plăcintă family continues the Latin word, while баница itself is Slavic. The Bulgarian dishes are given descriptions, not forced coinages.

Classical phrases at the table: I’m hungry / have some more / no, thank you / it’s in the oven

Ēsuriō hercle! · Benignē.

Classical quotationsFamily phrases
  • Ēsuriō hercle. — I’m starving, really! (Plaut. Cas. 801). Said before breakfast.
  • Vēscere, sōdēs. — Jam satis est. — At tū, quantum vīs, tolle. — Benignē. — Eat, please. — I’ve had enough. — Take as much as you like. — No, thank you (Hor. Epist. I 7, 15–16). Here benignē is a polite refusal.
  • Jam dūdum animus est in patinīs. — My mind has been on the dishes for ages (Ter. Eun. 816); said while waiting at the oven.
  • Bonum sit! — May it turn out well! (Verg. Ecl. 8, 106, via Ranieri); said as the dish goes into the oven.
  • Ēn erit umquam ille diēs? — Will that day ever come? (Ecl. 8, 7–8); for waiting at the oven.
  • Īte domum saturae, venit Hesperus. — Go home full, the evening star is coming (Ecl. 10, 77); said after the meal.
  • Utramque in furnum mīsērunt. «Bonum sit!» inquit pater. — They put both in the oven. “May it turn out well!” said Dad. (Fābula IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Jamdūdum ēsuriō, tata! — I’ve been hungry for ages, Dad! (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).

These are quotations, and their sources are given. Fābulae II and IV and the back-matter lists of “locī memoriā tenendī” suggest when to use them with Theo.

  • lectus, lectī m. — bed or couch; pulvīnus, pulvīnī m. — cushion or pillow; cervīcal, cervīcālis n. — pillow for the head.
  • lōdīx, lōdīcis f. — blanket; strāgulum, strāgulī n. — bed covering, a broader term.
  • linteum, linteī n. — linen cloth; applied to a bedsheet; linteum lectī specifies a sheet for the bed.
  • Pulvīnum cape. — Take the pillow.
  • Tē lōdīce tegam? — Shall I cover you with the blanket?
  • For the ordinary modern blanket, Traupman (p. 122), Morgan–Owens and Vicipaedia agree on lōdīx. Lōdīcem affer. — Bring the blanket.

Curtain / rod / pole / track

aulaeum, aulaeī n.

Ancient wordsModern formations
  • aulaeum, aulaeī n. — curtain, hanging or drapery [Ancient Latin].
  • virga aulaeī — curtain rod; our preferred transparent formation for a slender cylindrical rod, such as the metal rod used with curtain rings.
  • pertica aulaeī — curtain pole; useful especially when the support is longer, thicker or more pole-like.
  • annulus aulaeī — curtain ring; plural annulī aulaeī.
  • fulcrum virgae — bracket/support for the rod; plural fulcra virgae.
  • virga extensilis aulaeī — extendable/telescoping curtain rod.
  • canālis aulaeī — curtain track/rail; a transparent modern formation based on ancient canālis “channel, groove.” Use this for a track system rather than a free-standing cylindrical rod.
  • Aulaeum ex virgā pendet. — The curtain hangs from the rod. Annulōs in virgam indūc. — Put the rings onto the rod.
  • Evidence note: the individual nouns are ancient. The compounds virga aulaeī, pertica aulaeī and canālis aulaeī are transparent modern formations; no strong lexicographic evidence was found that any one of them is an established traditional term. For the photographed slender metal rod, virga aulaeī is preferred.

Tools, fasteners & household repair · English / Български

Officīna et īnstrūmenta

17 entries

Basic hand tools

īnstrūmentum, īnstrūmentī n.

Ancient Latin

English → Български: tool — инструмент; hammer — чук; nail — пирон; saw — трион; file — пила; chisel — длето; axe / hatchet — брадва / брадвичка; spade / shovel — права лопата / лопата

  • īnstrūmentum, īnstrūmentī n. — tool, implement or instrument; an excellent general word for a practical tool.
  • malleus, malleī m. — hammer, mallet or maul.
  • clāvus, clāvī m. — nail.
  • serra, serrae f. — saw.
  • līma, līmae f. — file.
  • scalprum, scalprī n. — sharp cutting tool, especially a chisel or graver.
  • secūris, secūris f. — axe or hatchet.
  • pāla, pālae f. — spade; also usable more broadly for a shovel in later lexicographic tradition. Exact English distinctions depend on the form of the tool.
  • Malleum mihi dā. — Give me the hammer. Clāvum malleō fīge. — Drive the nail with the hammer.

Screw / screwdriver / wrench

cōchlea / cochlea, -ae f.

Ancient wordNeo-Latin technical useVariable quantity

English → Български: screw — винт; screwdriver — отвертка; powered drill-driver — винтоверт; wrench / spanner — гаечен ключ; adjustable wrench — раздвижен гаечен ключ

  • cōchlea / cochlea, -ae f. — screw. Ancient cochlea already denotes spiral and screw mechanisms; later technical Latin applies it directly to the modern threaded fastener.
  • Lewis & Short marks the first vowel of cochlea as variable (cō̆-), so this lexicon does not pretend that one quantity is uniquely correct.
  • vertitōrium, -ī n. — screwdriver [Neo-Latin lexicographic term; Helfer]. Morgan–Owens also records the descriptive īnstrūmentum cochleīs extorquendīs from Latham.
  • clāvis mēchanica — wrench / spanner [Neo-Latin lexicographic term]. clāvis Anglica is also recorded for a universal/adjustable wrench.
  • Modern Latin sources do not maintain a single universally standardized terminology for every modern screwdriver, screw and wrench subtype; specific types should therefore be formed or selected case by case.
  • Cochleam vertitōriō intorque. — Screw the screw in with the screwdriver. Clāvem mēchanicam affer. — Bring the wrench.
  • vertitōrium ēlectricum — powered screwdriver / drill-driver; винтоверт. Our descriptive qualification of the recorded noun; a drill-driver also drills, whereas a hand screwdriver is an отвертка.
Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: coclea / cochlea · Morgan–Owens: screw · Morgan–Owens: screwdriver · Morgan–Owens: wrench

Nut / screw thread / screw actions

mātrix cochleae

Neo-Latin lexicographic evidenceVariable terminology

English → Български: nut — гайка; bolt — болт; screw thread — резба; screw in — завивам; tighten — затягам; unscrew — развивам

  • mātrix cochleae — nut used with a bolt or screw; Morgan–Owens cites Scheller’s 1783 lexicon. cochlea fēmina is another recorded expression.
  • rūgae f. pl. — screw threads in later technical lexicography. The connection is old: Pliny uses singular rūga for a female screw.
  • cochleam intorquēre — turn/screw a screw in [18th-century evidence].
  • firmāre cochleā — fasten or tighten with a screw [19th-century / Helfer].
  • cochleam retorquēre — unscrew; cochleam evolvere is another recorded expression.
  • The modern English distinction between screw and bolt is not mapped consistently onto one fixed pair of Latin nouns in the sources checked. cochlea is therefore kept broad here rather than creating a false precision.
Sources & evidence

Morgan–Owens: nut used with bolt · Morgan–Owens: screw / bolt (verb) · Morgan–Owens: screw in / tighten · Morgan–Owens: unscrew · Lewis & Short: matrix · Lewis & Short: ruga

Drill / boring tool

terēbra / terebra, -ae f.

Ancient LatinModern extensionVariable quantity

English → Български: drill — бормашина; drill bit — свредло; auger / gimlet — свредел; electric drill — електрическа бормашина; drill-driver — винтоверт

  • terēbra / terebra, -ae f. — boring tool, auger or gimlet in ancient Latin; the natural inherited word for a modern drill.
  • Lewis & Short marks the second vowel as variable (tĕrē̆bra). Both forms are therefore shown rather than silently choosing one reconstruction.
  • terebra ēlectrica — electric drill [our transparent modern extension of the ancient tool-name].
  • Morgan–Owens also records perforaculum and furfuraculum; for ordinary speech we prefer the historically established terebra.
  • Terēbram affer. — Bring the drill. This example adopts the long-vowel variant explicitly listed above.
  • terebra māchinālis — power drill; механизирана бормашина. Recorded by Morgan–Owens, citing Eichenseer; the inherited noun retains its variable vowel quantity.

Ancient wordNeo-Latin extensionWorking formation

Ancient LatinNeo-Latin lexicographic evidence

  • lībella, lībellae f. — level / levelling instrument; an unusually good ancient match for the modern spirit-level function. Pliny, NH 7.198 credits its invention, with the square, to Theodorus of Samos: normam autem et lībellam et tornum et clāvem Theodōrus Samius. See plane / square.

Adze / hew / dress timber / box of nails

ascia, asciae f.; dolō, dolāre

Ancient Latin
  • ascia, asciae f. — adze, the carpenter’s axe for dressing timber; тесла. Lewis & Short: “an axe for hewing wood, a carpenter’s axe”; secūris is the ordinary axe.
  • Pliny, NH 7.198 makes Daedalus the inventor of carpentry and of its first tools: fabricam māteriāriam Daedalus et in eā serram, asciam, perpendiculum, terebram. The square and the level go to Theodorus of Samos (see plane / square).
  • Pliny, NH 16.207: lime wood blunts adzes fastest, mollissima tilia … quod citissimē asciās retundat.
  • Vitruvius 7.2.2: the adze also tests slaked lime, sūmātur ascia et, quemadmodum māteria dolātur, sīc calx in lacū mācerāta asciētur; if the lime clings to the iron like glue, it is ready for plastering.
  • dolō, dolāre, dolāvī, dolātum — hew, chip into shape with an axe or adze; дялам. Cato, Agr. 14 dolābit, secābit, of the contractor’s timber work; Cicero, Div. 2.86 (Lewis & Short).
  • The Fābula VII gloss on ascia: secūris fabrī quā trabēs dolantur.
  • capsa clāvōrum — box of nails; pulsō, pulsāre — strike, knock. For the plane and square, the trowel and the plumb line see their own entries; hammer, saw, nails and chisel are in the basic tool entry.
  • Asciam mihi dā. — Give me the adze. Дай ми теслата. Faber tignum asciā dolat. — The carpenter is dressing the beam with the adze. Майсторът дяла гредата с теслата. Composed examples.
  • malleus, serra, ascia, quam Bulgarī teslam vocant, secūris, terebra, scalprum, rēgula, norma, forceps, runcīna, trulla, quā tēctōrēs tēctōrium indūcunt, līnea cum perpendiculō, capsa clāvōrum — hammer, saw, the adze the Bulgarians call tesla, axe, drill, chisel, ruler, square, pincers, plane, the trowel plasterers spread plaster with, a plumb line, a box of nails (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • quī trabem asciā dolābat — who was dressing a beam with the adze (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • «Asciam nōvī!» inquit Theodōrus. «Asciam volō!» — I know the adze! I want the adze! (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • Dā mihi, ōrō, ūtendum malleum, tata! — Lend me the hammer, please, Dad! (after Pont. Progymn. I 35; quoted in Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).

Hook / hook onto / catch with a hook

uncus, uncī m.; hāmus, hāmī m.

Ancient wordsComposed descriptions
  • uncus, uncī m. — general hook. hāmus, hāmī m. — hook, especially a fishhook. Traupman gives a clothes hook as uncus vestiārius (p. 123) and a fishhook as hāmus (p. 47).
  • prehendō, prehendere — catch or take hold of; uncō prehendere — catch with a hook, our descriptive phrase.
  • affīgō, affīgere, affīxī, affīxum — fasten or attach; uncō affīgere — fasten with a hook, our descriptive phrase. uncō can also be the dative “to a hook”; the construction and context determine the relation.
  • Hoc huic uncō affīge. — Hook this onto this hook / attach this to this hook. Uncum affer. — Bring the hook.
  • aduncus, adunca, aduncum — hook-shaped / hooked. bacillum aduncum — a hooked stick; our reader series uses the diminutive bacillum for Theo’s stick. Livy 1.18.7 has baculum sine nōdō aduncum, but there it is the augur’s crook, the lituus, not an ordinary stick. A stick can have a hooked end without being a purpose-made hook.
  • suspendō, suspendere — hang up / suspend. Theodōrus bacillum aduncum ex trānsversāriō māchinae suspendit. — Theo hung the hooked stick from the scaffold’s crossbar. Our composed example for hooking the stick over a scaffolding bar and leaving it hanging. trānsversārium is Vitruvius’s crosspiece (see the scaffold-members entry); a scaffold tube is not a vectis (lever, crowbar). For suspendere ex + ablative compare Vergil, G. 2.389 oscilla ex altā suspendunt mollia pīnū.
  • Bacillō aduncō trānsversārium prehendit. — He caught / hooked the crossbar with the hooked stick. Our composed example when he keeps holding the stick and catches the bar with its curved end.
  • affīgere emphasizes attachment or fastening; it is not a universal equivalent of English “hook.” uncus need not name a separately manufactured item, but describing this whole object as a bacillum aduncum is clearer. Choose the verb according to the action and result.

The two English verb senses are expressed compositionally; neither phrase is presented as a separately verified technical headword.

Plaster / lime / mortar / sand / cement / concrete

tēctōrium, tēctōriī n.

Ancient wordsModern technical senses
  • tēctōrium, tēctōriī n. — plaster / plaster coating; мазилка. Traupman p. 168; Palladius discusses applying and levelling it.
  • calx, calcis f. — lime; вар. Do not silently equate lime with modern cement; Traupman’s English cement gloss is too broad for buying modern building materials.
  • harēna, harēnae f. — sand; пясък.
  • harēnātum, harēnātī n. — lime-and-sand mortar; варо-пясъчен разтвор. Traupman p. 168, and also classical: Cato, Agr. 18.7 dē glāreā et calce harēnātō; Vitruvius 7.3.5; Pliny, NH 36.176 (Lewis & Short). Mortar is строителен разтвор; хоросан commonly means lime-based mortar.
  • lithocolla, lithocollae f. — cement; цимент. Recorded for modern cemento in the Vatican’s public abridgement. The unmarked modern stem vowels are not claimed to have independently established quantities.
  • opus caementīcium, operis caementīciī n. — concrete; бетон. The modern name for Roman concrete, built on Vitruvius’s caementīcius, “of rubble stones” (in caementīciīs autem strūctūrīs, 2.4.1; parietibus caementīciīs, 2.8.17); used here for modern concrete too. Traupman p. 168 has concrētum, which is not used: classical concrētus means “thickened, congealed”.
  • Classical mortar and rubble terms: māteria, māteriae f. — in Vitruvius also the mixed mortar (2.5.1; 2.8.2); caementa, caementōrum n. pl. — rough quarry stones / rubble laid in mortar; ломен камък; rūdus, rūderis n. — broken stone mixed with lime for floors; statūmen n. — the bottom bedding layer of a floor (Vitruvius 7.1.1).
  • Tēctōrium parietī indūcunt. — They are applying plaster to the wall. Полагат мазилка върху стената.

Recorded Neo-LatinDescriptive qualificationsWorking formation
  • īnsulātiō, īnsulātiōnis f. — insulation; изолация. Morgan–Owens records insulatio, citing Helfer; the brief entry does not specify a complete thermal-insulation system.
  • īnsulātiō thermica — thermal insulation; топлоизолация. Our explicit thermal qualifier, not an independently verified complete entry.
  • tabula ad calōrem retinendum — insulation board, described as a board for retaining heat; топлоизолационна плоча. Our functional description. For an individual panel, tabula, tabulae f. is a useful broad noun; the precise material should be specified separately.
  • tabula spūmea; tabulae spūmeae f. — EPS insulation board (expanded polystyrene); EPS плоча / стиропор. Our working formation, not an attested term, built on classical spūmeus, spūmea, spūmeum “foamy” (Vergil, Ovid, Pliny). Gloss: tabula levissima ex māteriā artificiōsā spūmeā facta, quae parietibus forīs affīgitur, ut domus hieme calōrem retineat et aestāte frīgus. The common boards on site are black, graphite EPS (графитен EPS / графитен стиропор), not white.
  • mūnīmentum adversus frīgus — protection against the cold; parietēs adversus frīgus mūnīre — insulate the walls. Our functional descriptions, preferable in narration because īnsulātiō collides with īnsula. Classical model for the function: Columella 9.7.4 quod tegumen cum frīgora et pluviās tum et aestūs arcet.
  • Nōlī hanc tabulam perforāre. — Don’t make holes in this board. Не пробивай тази плоча.

Gravel

glārea, glāreae f.

Ancient Latin
  • glārea, glāreae f. — gravel; a collective material noun. Lewis & Short cites road-building use, including Livy 41.27.5. Morgan–Owens also lists it.

Dirt / soil / grime

terra, terrae f.; sordēs, sordium f. pl.

Ancient LatinSense distinctions
  • terra, terrae f. — dirt as earth or soil; the ordinary material dug out of a trench.
  • sordēs, sordium f. pl. — dirt as grime or filth. A singular also exists; the plural is the useful everyday form given here.

Mound / pile (noun) / pile up (verb)

tumulus, tumulī m.; acervus, acervī m.

Ancient LatinComposed prompts
  • tumulus, tumulī m. — raised heap of earth, mound or small hill. The noun also has a burial-mound sense, prominent in poetry (Vergil, Ecl. 5.42 tumulum facite), but is not restricted to graves; a hillock is larger than a child’s heap.
  • cumulus, cumulī m. — heap; our recommendation for a child’s heap of sand, gravel or dirt. Vergil, G. 1.105 cumulōsque … harēnae; Ovid, Met. 14.137 pulveris … cumulum.
  • acervus, acervī m. — heap or pile. acervus terrae — pile of dirt; acervus lapidum — pile of stones.
  • cumulō, cumulāre, cumulāvī, cumulātum — heap / pile up; transitive. Lewis & Short gives material objects including sand, snow and logs, and marks the physical sense as mostly post-Augustan. coacervō, coacervāre, coacervāvī, coacervātum — heap together.
  • Terram hīc cumulā. — Pile the dirt here. Lapidēs in acervum congere. — Heap the stones into a pile. congerō, congerere, congessī, congestum — bring or heap together. congestus, congestūs m. — a heaping up, a heap; Seneca, Const. 12.2 has children who in lītoribus harēnae congestū simulācra domuum excitant.
  • This is “pile” meaning a heap, not a foundation pile driven into the ground.

Scaffold / scaffolding / framework

māchina, māchinae f.

Ancient wordsModern applicationsDescriptive phrases
  • māchina, māchinae f. — scaffold / scaffolding for building, the Roman word. Digest 13.6.5.7 (Ulpian): a plasterer lent out falls dē māchinā; the risk differs if he was lent to work dē plānō, on the ground, or if the scaffold was minus dīligenter … ligāta or failed through fūnium perticārumque vetustāte. Vitruvius 7.2.2 māchinīs comparātīs (scaffolds set up for vaulting rooms); Vitruvius 10.1.1 scānsōriae māchinae, built tignīs statūtīs et trānsversāriīs conligātīs. Lewis & Short I.B.3 also cites Pliny 19.2.8 §30 (NH 19.30), but there māchinīs aedificātiōnum means building machinery such as hoists, which is weak evidence for scaffolding. The noun is broader than modern English “machine.” Morgan–Owens also lists it under scaffolding.
  • arrēctāria, arrēctāriōrum n. pl.; trānsversāria, trānsversāriōrum n. pl. — uprights and crosspieces, Vitruvius’s names for the members; see the scaffold-members entry.
  • compāgēs, compāgis f. — joining, joint, framework (Lewis & Short: “a joining together, connection, joint, structure,” used of the body and the state). Classically it never names a builder’s scaffold; the scaffolding sense is modern lexicographic (Morgan–Owens). Useful as a gloss word, not as the narrative noun.
  • māchina ex fistulīs ferreīs — scaffolding made of iron tubes; our descriptive phrase for the modern construction-site object.
  • Operārius in māchinā stat. — The worker is standing on the scaffold. Māchinam juxtā domum cōnstruunt. — They are assembling the scaffolding beside the house. Dē plānō lūde, nōn in māchinā. — Play on the ground, not on the scaffold; after the Digest’s dē plānō. These sentences are composed.
  • pēgma, pēgmatis n. is another ancient framework/machinery noun, especially for theatrical stage machinery and board fixtures. Its ancient examples do not by themselves establish the modern tube-and-clamp construction sense; māchina has the clearer explicit builder’s-scaffold entry.

Scaffold pole / upright / crossbar / diagonal brace

arrēctārium, arrēctāriī n.; trānsversārium, trānsversāriī n.

Ancient wordsModern applicationsDescriptive phrases
  • arrēctārium, arrēctāriī n., usually plural arrēctāria — upright, standard. Vitruvius 2.8.20 arrēctāriōrum et trānsversāriōrum dispositiōne and 7.3.11 in arrēctāriīs et trānsversāriīs, of the posts of timber-framed walls; 10.13.4 of the uprights of siege towers. Lewis & Short: “the upright posts of a wall.” Applied here to the steel standards of a tube scaffold.
  • trānsversārium, trānsversāriī n. — crosspiece; ledger / transom. Vitruvius 10.1.1 tignīs statūtīs et trānsversāriīs conligātīs; 2.8.20; Caesar, BC 2.15 has tigna trānsversāria (Lewis & Short). One noun serves both horizontal functions; Latin does not distinguish ledger and transom.
  • pertica, perticae f. — pole; the Digest’s word for the poles of a lashed Roman scaffold (13.6.5.7 fūnium perticārumque vetustāte).
  • fistula, fistulae f.; fistula ferrea; tubus ferreus — tube; iron tube. Material glosses for the hollow steel member, not member names; classically a fistula is first a (lead) water pipe, and tubus a pipe. For a wooden pole or beam, asser, asseris m. is ancient; the shape and material determine which noun fits.
  • fistula ad perpendiculum posita — upright / vertical tube, literally a tube placed plumb; our description; the classical member name is arrēctārium. Ancient ad perpendiculum means vertically / perpendicularly.
  • ferrum trānsversum; ferrī trānsversī n. — crossbar / horizontal metal bar. Morgan–Owens and Traupman record it in gymnastics; applying it to this scaffold bar is our contextual extension. fistula trānsversa specifies a hollow cross-tube. The classical member name is trānsversārium.
  • fulcīmentum, fulcīmentī n. — prop, stay or support; an ancient post-classical noun. fulcīmentum oblīquum — diagonal brace, our functional description. oblīquus, oblīqua, oblīquum means slanting / diagonal.
  • Theodōrus bacillum aduncum ex trānsversāriō māchinae suspendit. — Theo hung the hooked stick from the scaffold’s crossbar. Our full composed version of the site example.

Scaffold platform / deck / plank / guardrails / base plate / ladder

tabulātum, tabulātī n.; tabula, tabulae f.

Ancient wordsModern applicationsDescriptive phrases
  • tabulātum, tabulātī n. — planked flooring, floor or platform; applied here to the scaffold’s working deck. The floor/storey sense also appears in the existing house-layout entry; Vitruvius 10.13.4 has a siege tower tabulātōrum decem. Vergil, A. 9.530 turris erat vastō suspectū et pontibus altīs: pontēs, high gangways, a poetic model for walk-boards.
  • tabula, tabulae f. — plank / board; an individual wooden plank of the deck. A metal deck is a modern application of the platform vocabulary, not evidence that ancient platforms used the same fittings.
  • repāgula, repāgulōrum n. pl. — bars / barriers, ancient especially for door bars; our functional extension to guardrails. ferrum trānsversum ad marginem tabulātī positum describes one metal rail placed at the edge of the deck. Neither is asserted to be a standardized modern scaffold-component term. Closer ancient words for a parapet: pluteus, pluteī m. — breastwork, parapet on towers (Caesar, BG 7.41, per Lewis & Short); lōrīca, lōrīcae f. — breastwork, parapet (Caesar, per Lewis & Short).
  • lāmina, lāminae f. — plate / sheet. lāmina sub fistulā posita — base plate under a scaffold tube; our description, not a verified technical compound.
  • scālae, scālārum f. pl. — ladder / stairs; gradus, gradūs m. — step or ladder rung. See the existing stairs / ladder entry.
  • Operārius super tabulātum ambulat. — The worker is walking on the platform. This is vocabulary for describing the scene, not an assembly specification.

Scaffold joint / coupler / assemble / brace / dismantle

jūnctūra, jūnctūrae f.; cōnstruō, cōnstruere

Ancient wordsModern applicationsDescriptive phrases
  • jūnctūra, jūnctūrae f. — joining / joint / connection; the ancient general noun is applied here to the joint between scaffold members.
  • vinculum, vinculī n. — fastening / bond / tie. vinculum quō duae fistulae conjunguntur — a fastening by which two tubes are joined; our descriptive “coupler / clamp.” It describes the function rather than claiming a specific modern coupler design had an ancient name.
  • ligō, ligāre, ligāvī, ligātum — tie, lash; the Digest’s verb for a Roman scaffold (13.6.5.7 māchinae … nōn ab ipsō ligātae). retinācula, retināculōrum n. pl. — ropes, stays, ties (Cato, Vergil, Vitruvius, per Lewis & Short); applied here to the ties anchoring the scaffold to the wall.
  • cōnstruō, cōnstruere, cōnstrūxī, cōnstrūctum — construct / build; here assemble. ērigō, ērigere — raise / erect. conjungō, conjungere — connect / join together.
  • firmō, firmāre — secure / make firm; fulciō, fulcīre — prop up / brace / support. dissolvō, dissolvere, dissolvī, dissolūtum — take apart / dismantle; the verb has ancient use for taking apart a bridge.
  • Fistulās inter sē conjungunt. — They are connecting the tubes together. Māchinam fulcīmentīs firmant. — They are securing the scaffold with braces. Māchinam dissolvunt. — They are dismantling the scaffold.
  • The verbs are ancient; the full modern-scaffold applications and sample sentences are ours. The ancient member names (arrēctāria, trānsversāria) are attested; only the steel coupler and adjustable base jack are modern, and no exact Latin names for them have been verified in the named sources.

Ancient nounsDescriptive roof shape

Storey / top floor / attic / furnished loft

tabulātum, tabulātī n.; subtēgulāneum, -ī n.

Ancient nounModern lexicographic useModern application
  • tabulātum, tabulātī n. — storey / floor of a building; also boarded flooring; етаж; също дъсчен под. Traupman p. 125; ancient storey sense in Lewis & Short.

Ancient LatinModern room useDescriptive furniture terms

Classically a room furnished with seats, for conversation: Vitruvius 5.11.2 exhedrae spatiōsae, habentēs sēdēs (so spelt in the Latin Library text), and in Cicero the room where the speakers of a dialogue sit and talk (de Or. 3.17; N.D. 1.15; Lewis & Short).   • Not sessōrium: Traupman (pp. 124–125) gives it for “living room”, but its ancient senses are “seat, stool” (Caelius Aurelianus) and, in a single passage, “dwelling” (Petronius 77.4 vīperae hujus sessōrium) (Lewis & Short).

Ground level / basement / terrace / wing / extension / sand pit / lime kiln

plānō pede; hypogēum, hypogēī n.

Ancient LatinModern applications
  • plānō pede — at ground level, entered without steps; на нивото на терена. Vitruvius 6.8.1 aedificia quae plānō pede īnstituuntur (Lewis & Short cites the older numbering 6.11); also 7.4.1 conclāvibus, quae plānō pede fuerint.
  • hypogēum, hypogēī n. (also hypogaeum) — basement, underground vault; сутерен / мазе. Vitruvius 6.8.1 sīn autem hypogēa concamarātiōnēsque īnstituentur, fundātiōnēs eōrum fierī dēbent crassiōrēs. It can also mean a burial vault (Petronius 111.2); on a building site the Vitruvian sense is clear. For Theo, cella subterrānea.
  • Hīc plānō pede intrāmus; illīc dēscendimus in hypogēum. — Here we walk straight in; over there we go down to the basement. Тук влизаме направо; там слизаме в сутерена. Composed.
  • sōlārium, sōlāriī n. — roof terrace, sunny flat roof or balcony; тераса. Lewis & Short: “a part of the house exposed to the sun, a flat house-top, a terrace”; Plautus, Mil. 340 neque sōlārium neque hortum; Suetonius, Claud. 10.1. The same noun also means a sundial. subdiālia, subdiālium n. pl. — open-air terraces (Pliny, NH 36.186).
  • diaeta, diaetae f. — a suite or wing of rooms, a pavilion (post-Augustan, Lewis & Short); крило / самостоятелна част от къщата. Pliny, Ep. 2.17.20 diaeta est, amōrēs meī, rē vērā amōrēs: ipse posuī; Suetonius, Claud. 10.1. The same noun also means a medical diet.
  • adstruō (astruō), adstruere, adstrūxī, adstrūctum — build on, add a building to; пристроявам. Columella 1.5.10 cum veterī adstruitur recēns aedificium; Pliny, Ep. 9.7.4 astruendī. aedificium adstrūctum; pars domūs nova, veterī adstrūcta — the new wing / extension; пристройка. Avoid āla: in Vitruvius (6.3.4) the ālae are side rooms off the atrium, not wings.
  • arrēctāria et trānsversāria — uprights and crosspieces, Vitruvius’s names for framing members; see the scaffold-members entry.
  • harēnārium, harēnāriī n. — sand pit, a place where sand is dug; пясъчна кариера. Vitruvius 2.4.2 sīn autem nōn erunt harēnāria, unde fodiātur; also harēnāria, harēnāriae f. (Varro, Cicero). Not the playground sandpit; see the sandbox entry.
  • fornāx calcāria; fornācis calcāriae f. — lime kiln; варница. Cato, Agr. 38.1 fornācem calcāriam pedēs lātam X facitō, altam pedēs XX. For the lime-burner, calcārius, see the builders entry.

Work & responsibility

Labor et cūra

2 entries

Slack off / be idle

cessō, cessāre, cessāvī, cessātum

Ancient Latin
  • cessō, cessāre, cessāvī, cessātum — be idle, delay, loiter or stop doing something; the context determines whether this means shirking.
  • labōrem neglegō — neglect my work; sēgniter agō — act sluggishly; ōtiō mē dēdō — give myself over to idleness.
  • langueō, languēre, languī — be weak or languid; it does not by itself imply deliberate shirking. The earlier languēō incorrectly lengthened a vowel before another vowel.
  • Nōlī cessāre. — Don’t dawdle / stop slacking.
  • Tōtum diem cessat. — He idles all day / has been idling all day.
Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: cesso · Lewis & Short: langueo · Lewis & Short: neglego · Bennett: hidden quantities, with later corrections

Accountability / hold oneself accountable

ratiōnem reddere

Classical idiomDescriptive extension
  • ratiōnem reddere — give an account or answer for one’s conduct; ratiōnem factī suī / factōrum suōrum reddere — account for one’s own action or actions.
  • putāre / arbitrārī sibi ratiōnem reddendam esse — think oneself answerable; agnōscere sibi ratiōnem reddendam esse — acknowledge that one must give an account. These are descriptions of self-accountability using the Classical construction.
  • Cicero, Verr. 2.2.28: semper ita vīvāmus, ut ratiōnem reddendam nōbīs arbitrēmur.
  • ratiōnem ab aliquō reposcere — demand an account from someone; Caesar, BG 5.30: abs tē ratiōnem reposcent. Both passages are cited under ratiō in Lewis & Short.
  • sibi imputāre — attribute something to oneself; culpam in sē recipere / culpam agnōscere — accept or acknowledge blame. These imply more than neutral answerability.
  • cūram suscipere / in sē recipere — undertake responsibility prospectively. Modern respōnsābilitātem assumere / suscipere is a broader expression and is not a uniquely exact equivalent for self-accountability.
  • Ulixēs nōn agnōscit sibi dē eō quod accidit ratiōnem reddendam esse; culpam sociīs tribuit. — Odysseus does not acknowledge himself answerable for what happened; he assigns blame to his companions.
Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: ratio · Lewis & Short: imputo · Lewis & Short: agnosco · Lewis & Short: cura

Computing & programming

Ars computātrālis

23 entries

Programming

programmātiō, programmātiōnis f.

Neo-LatinVariable terminology
  • programmātiō, programmātiōnis f. — programming, a modern formation; not claimed to be a uniquely settled term.
  • programmō, programmāre, programmāvī, programmātum — program; programmātor, programmātōris m. — programmer; the modern Silva cites Vox Latina for these forms.
  • programmātrīx, programmātrīcis f. — a transparent feminine counterpart.
  • programmātūra, programmātūrae f. — another modern choice; programmātūra computātrālis — computer programming.
  • lingua programmātiōnis or lingua programmandī — a programming language, descriptive phrases rather than a claim of universal standardization.
Sources & evidence

Morgan–Owens: Silva

Software

programmātūra, programmātūrae f.

Neo-LatinWorking preference
  • programmātūra, programmātūrae f. — our convenient working term for software; its scope varies among modern users.
  • programma, programmatis n. (plural programmata, genitive plural programmatum) — program; the third-declension stem has short a. Thus corpus programmatum means a collection or body of programs.
  • partēs programmātiōnis is a reported lexical proposal, not our preferred everyday expression. The new Morgan–Owens entry actually displays the problematic partes programmationes; that spelling is not evidence for the corrected genitive’s exact attestation.
  • apparātūra, apparātūrae f. — equipment or hardware as a modern working term; it is not the only possible choice.
Sources & evidence

Morgan–Owens: software · Morgan–Owens: Silva · Lewis & Short: programma

Source code

cōdex fontālis

Working formation
  • cōdex fontālis — our working expression for source code; no claim of established major-source usage.
  • cōdex, cōdicis m. — ancient book or tablet; computing “code” is a modern extension.
  • fontālis, fontāle — pertaining to a source, a post-Classical adjective; fōns, fontis m. — source or spring. The noun’s nominative ō is long before ns; it is not mechanically carried into fontis.

Merge

conjungō, conjungere, conjūnxī, conjūnctum

Ancient wordsModern extension
  • conjungō, conjungere, conjūnxī, conjūnctum — join or unite; extended to merging code.
  • conjūnctiō, conjūnctiōnis f. — joining or union; a descriptive name for a merge.
  • These are ancient words applied to a modern operation, not verified Git terminology. Preserve literal command names such as merge when discussing syntax.

Pull request

petītiō conjungendī

Working formation
  • petītiō conjungendī — our functional description “request to merge,” not an established Latin GitHub label.
  • petītiō, petītiōnis f. — request; conjungendī is a genitive gerund, “of joining.” It describes the proposed merge, not literally the Git pull operation.

Development cycle

cursus ēlabōrātiōnis

Working formation

  • cursus, cursūs m. — course or progression; ēlabōrātiō, ēlabōrātiōnis f. — elaboration or working out.

Ancient wordsModern extension

  • scrībō, scrībere, scrīpsī, scrīptum — write.

Commit

cōnsignō, cōnsignāre, cōnsignāvī, cōnsignātum

Ancient wordsModern extension
  • cōnsignō, cōnsignāre, cōnsignāvī, cōnsignātum — seal or record; applied here to committing a version.
  • cōnsignātiō, cōnsignātiōnis f. — recording or registration; our descriptive noun for a commit.
  • The Git meaning is a working extension. Preserve commit in literal commands.

Some older dictionaries lengthen the i before gn. That reading is disputed; no general rule of vowel lengthening before gn is applied here.

Ancient wordsModern extension

Code review

Technical noun relationships

genitive

  • Use ordinary Latin case syntax to make the relationship between technical nouns explicit: recōgnitiō cōdicis, cursus ēlabōrātiōnis.
  • The grammaticality of a phrase does not establish that it is idiomatic or widely used technical Latin; our new computing phrases remain labelled as working formations.
  • Preserve exact commands, filenames, branch names and protocol tokens where translation would alter their identity.

Project / plan / undertaking

opus, operis n.; cōnsilium, cōnsiliī n.

Ancient wordsModern application
  • opus, operis n. — work or undertaking; our everyday choice for a project being carried out. Plural opera, operum n. pl.. cōnsilium, cōnsiliī n. — plan, intention or design; useful when the planned undertaking is the focus.
  • Recovered from our 24 September 2026 discussion: both words were proposed, and Jack used Opus incipiāmus. These are contextual choices, not a claim that either word always corresponds to every English use of “project.”
  • Opus incipiāmus. — Let’s begin the project. Hoc opus suscipiāmus. — Let’s undertake this project. In hōc opere labōrō. — I’m working on this project.
  • Quid dē hōc cōnsiliō putās? — What do you think of this plan? Cōnsilium investīgātiōnis — a research plan; a descriptive phrase.
Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: opus · Lewis & Short: consilium. Dictionary links support the component words; the modern technical expressions are labelled separately.

QA / quality assurance / quality testing

cūrātiō quālitātis; probātiō quālitātis

Ancient wordsWorking formations
  • cūrātiō, cūrātiōnis f. — care, oversight or management; quālitās, quālitātis f. — quality, property or character. cūrātiō quālitātis is our descriptive expression for the broader work of quality assurance.
  • probātiō, probātiōnis f. — testing, inspection or examination; probātiō quālitātis — quality testing. Testing is one part of QA, so these two phrases are not exact synonyms.
  • Both expressions recover proposals from our 21 September 2026 conversation. The dictionary sources establish the component words and their older senses; they do not establish these complete phrases as standardized software terminology. Classical quālitās does not by itself mean “high quality.”
  • Programma probandum est. — The program needs testing. Quālitātem programmātūrae cūrō. — I look after software quality.
Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: curatio · Lewis & Short: qualitas · Lewis & Short: probatio. Dictionary links support the component words; the modern technical expressions are labelled separately.

Tester / QA tester

probātor, probātōris m.; probātrīx, probātrīcis f.

Ancient nounModern application
  • probātor, probātōris m. — approver; also examiner in ecclesiastical Latin. Applied here to a software tester. probātrīx, probātrīcis f. — our transparent feminine formation; its software use is not independently verified.
  • probātor programmatum — tester of programs; probātrīx programmatum — a female tester of programs. programmatum is the genitive plural of programma, programmatis n., with short stem a.
  • artifex probātiōnis quālitātis — a longer descriptive proposal from the earlier conversation for a quality-testing specialist. artifex, artificis m./f. denotes a skilled practitioner; it is not an established translation of the job title “QA engineer.”
  • Probātor mendum invēnit. — The tester found a bug.

Lewis & Short: probator · Lewis & Short: programma · Lewis & Short: artifex. Dictionary links support the component words; the modern technical expressions are labelled separately.

Testing types / automated / manual / regression / integration / unit / acceptance

genera probātiōnum

Working formations
  • probātiō automatica — automated testing; probātiō manuālis — manual testing. These recover our earlier proposals; the quantity of every modern technical stem is not independently established here.
  • probātiō regressiōnis — regression testing; a technical calque whose meaning must be supplied by context: checking that changes have not broken previously working behaviour.
  • probātiō integrātiōnis — integration testing; probātiō ūnitātis — a unit test / testing of a unit; probātiō acceptātiōnis — acceptance testing. These are working technical calques, not independently attested standards.
  • probātiōnēs exercēre — carry out tests; probātiōnēs repetere — repeat the tests. Post mūtātiōnem cōdicis probātiōnēs repetāmus. — Let’s repeat the tests after changing the code.

Lewis & Short: probatio. Dictionary links support the component words; the modern technical expressions are labelled separately.

Test case / test condition / expected and actual result

cāsus probātiōnis; exitus exspectātus

Ancient wordsWorking formations
  • cāsus, cāsūs m. — case or occurrence; cāsus probātiōnis — test case, our descriptive calque. condiciō, condiciōnis f. — condition; condiciō probātiōnis — test condition.
  • exitus, exitūs m. — outcome or result; exitus exspectātus — expected result; exitus repertus — observed / actual result, literally the result found. These recover the practical distinctions from the earlier QA discussion.
  • The earlier alternative exitus rēālis is a modern formation; exitus repertus makes the intended “observed result” more explicit. None of these full expressions is presented as established QA terminology.
  • Exitus repertus ab exspectātō differt. — The actual result differs from the expected result.

Bug report / defect / report a bug / fix a bug

relātiō dē mendō; vitium, vitiī n.

Ancient wordsModern application
  • relātiō, relātiōnis f. — report or account; relātiō dē mendō — bug report, our descriptive phrase. The earlier discussion used relātiō dē vitiō; both describe a report about a fault.
  • vitium, vitiī n. — defect or fault, applied here to software; plural vitia. Our existing preferred everyday “bug” is mendum, mendī n.; keeping that choice makes related phrases consistent.
  • mendum invenīre / reperīre — find a bug; dē mendō referre — report a bug; mendum ēmendāre — fix a bug. Earlier alternatives: vitium invenīre, vitium corrigere.
  • corrēctiō, corrēctiōnis f. — correction; ēmendātiō mendī — correction of a bug. Dē hōc mendō jam rettulī. — I’ve already reported this bug.

Reproduce a bug / reproduction steps

mendum iterum efficere

Working descriptions
  • mendum iterum efficere — make the bug occur again; efficiō, efficere, effēcī, effectum — bring about or cause. This is our explicit working description of reproducing a software bug.
  • gradūs ad mendum iterum efficiendum — steps to reproduce a bug; gradus, gradūs m. — step. Eīsdem gradibus adhibitīs, idem mendum iterum accidit. — Following the same steps, the same bug occurs again.
  • The earlier QA conversation used “reproducere vitium” and “gradūs ad vitium reproducendum.” That wording is recorded here as a prior proposal, not as an independently verified technical term; the preferred description above avoids relying on that verb’s modern technical sense.
  • Hoc mendum iterum efficere nōn possum. — I can’t reproduce this bug.

Lewis & Short: efficio · Lewis & Short: gradus · Lewis & Short: mendum. Dictionary links support the component words; the modern technical expressions are labelled separately.

Metric / metrics / analytics / figures

index numericus; numerī; mēnsūra

Ancient wordsWorking extensions
  • index, indicis m. — indicator or pointer; index numericus, plural indicēs numericī — our working technical expression for numerical metrics. indicēs praecipuī — key metrics; indicēs incrēmentī — growth metrics.
  • numerus, numerī m., plural numerī — numbers or figures; our informal choice when thinking about the reported statistics. mēnsūra, mēnsūrae f. — measure or measurement; useful when the measure itself is the focus.
  • Recovered from our 16 October discussion. These are proposals, not a verified community standard. index also has other senses, including a list; the qualifier numericus can disambiguate. API resource names must be interpreted from the platform’s own definitions: some “metrics” resources describe tracked event types rather than numerical values.
  • Numerōs inspicere debeō. — I need to check the figures. Quōs indicēs observāmus? — Which metrics are we tracking?

Lewis & Short: index · Lewis & Short: numerus · Lewis & Short: mensura. Dictionary links support the component words; the modern technical expressions are labelled separately.

Mailing list / recipient list

catalogus dēstinātāriōrum

Working formation
  • catalogus, catalogī m. — catalogue or list; catalogus dēstinātāriōrum — our descriptive “recipient list” from the email-platform discussion. dēstinātārius, dēstinātāriī m. is modern vocabulary for a recipient; the full phrase is not claimed as an established platform label.
  • The computing glossary instead proposes grex Internetī for a mailing list. That emphasizes a group; an email-marketing platform’s stored list of recipients can be described more directly with catalogus. These alternatives need not name exactly the same kind of resource.
  • Catalogum inspiciam. — I’ll inspect the list. Hunc dēstinātārium catalogō adde. — Add this recipient to the list.
Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: catalogus · Vocabula computatralia: list. Dictionary links support the component words; the modern technical expressions are labelled separately.

API key / scopes / permissions / read access / full access

clāvis API; jūs legendī

Working descriptions
  • clāvis, clāvis f. — key; clāvis API — our working “API key.” Retain the technical abbreviation API when its exact identity matters. These descriptions supplement the email-platform discussion; they are not recovered quotations from an older vocabulary list.
  • jūs, jūris n. — right or permission; jūra clāvis API — the API key’s permissions. A scope defines a particular extent of authorization; “permissions” is useful ordinary wording, not an assertion that scope and permission are technically identical on every platform.
  • jūs legendī — read permission; jūs legendī et scrībendī — read-and-write permission. “Full access” may include additional actions, depending on the platform. omnia jūra — all permissions, when that is what the platform grants.
  • Hāc clāve numerōs legere mihi licet. — This key lets me read the figures. Hāc clāve data mūtāre mihi nōn licet. — This key does not let me change the data.
Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: clavis · Lewis & Short: jus · Lewis & Short: lego · Lewis & Short: scribo. Dictionary links support the component words; the modern technical expressions are labelled separately.

Computer / laptop / keyboard / screen / phone / app

computātrum, computātrī n. · computātrulum portābile

Neo-LatinLexicographic evidenceWorking formation
  • computātrum, computātrī n. — computer (Traupman 260); computātrulum portābile — laptop (261).
  • plēctrologium, plēctrologiī n. — keyboard (Traupman 261); quadrum vīsificum; quadrum, quadrī n. — screen (262).
  • programma, programmatis n.; programma compōnere — program; write a program (Traupman 262). Bugs, fixing and committing are in the existing programming entries.
  • tēlephōnum, tēlephōnī n. — telephone; tēlephōnī programma — phone app: a working phrase (locūtiō nostra).
  • Pater in tablīnum iit, jānuam clausit, computātrulum in mēnsā scrīptōriā aperuit — Dad went into the study, shut the door and opened his laptop on the desk (Fābula III, Apud avum et aviam).
  • quadrum vīsificum illūxit, plēctrologium crepitāre coepit — the screen lit up, the keyboard began to clatter (Fābula III, Apud avum et aviam).
  • «Programmata,» inquit, «in computātrulō compōnō …» — “I write programs,” he said, “on the laptop …” (Fābula III, Apud avum et aviam).
  • Mendum est sīcut lapillus in calceō tuō: nōn bene ambulās, dōnec lapillum invēneris et ējēceris. — A bug is like a pebble in your shoe: you can’t walk properly until you’ve found the pebble and thrown it out. (Fābula III, Apud avum et aviam).
